title: A prospective population cohort study of post-natal mental disorder in the rural region of Butajira, Ethiopia, to determine prevalence, predictors, natural course and associated adverse outcomes.
description: Post-natal mental disorder (PNMD) is increasingly recognised as a significant public health issue for infants as well as mothers in low-income countries. We will use the Self-Report Questionnaire to study PNMD in a rural community in Ethiopia characterised by high rates of infant malnutrition and mortality. 700 women will be recruited in the final trimester of pregnancy and they and their children followed through until one year post-partum. The study is powered to detect large (policy-relevant) effects of PNMD on infant mortality at one year, but will also allow ante-natal risk factors for PNMD (at 2 months), and effects of PNMD upon infant growth and development to be estimated with more precision than was possible in previous, smaller prospective studies. The Butajira Rural Health Project (three monthly surveillance of all households in a 37,000 catchment area) allows us to identify a representative population sample of pregnant women, and assures that recruitment and follow-up targets are feasible. Assessments will be completed by experienced Butajira Project survey interviewers. Child cognitive and motor development assessments (Bayley Scales) are time consuming and require special training. These will be complicated at one year on children of all those with PNMD at 2 months, and on a similar number of children of mothers without PNMD.

title: Historical and conceptual links between Pierre Janet and Eugen Bleuler's (1911) concept of schizophrenia: A preliminary exploration.
description: Historical and conceptual links between Pierre Janet and Eugen Bleuler's (1911) concept of schizophrenia: A preliminary exploration In the broadest terms, this project aims to explore the historical and conceptual roots of Eugen Bleuler's concept of schizophrenia, and its impact in Britain. The basic hypothesis is that the influence of Sigmund Freud on Bleuler's thinking has been overrated (including by Bleuler himself), with a corresponding devaluation of the extent to which Bleuler was influenced by Pierre Janet and his concepts, along with allied 'dissociationists' (such as Theodore Flournoy). The research attempts to trace the development not only of Bleuler's concept of schizophrenia, but also of the fundamental terms 'loosening' ('Lockerung') of associations, 'splitting' ('Spaltung') and complexes ('Komplex'). I am also seeking to trace Bleuler's contact with a variety of figures, and trace the significance of their influence on him, including Charcot, Forel, Wundt, Wernicke, Breuer, and, of course, Freud. Perhaps the most important is the influence of Carl Jung, Bleuler's colleague at the Burgholzi Hospital during the crucial years the concept of schizophrenia was being developed, and his 'second in command' for many years. The questions to address are: 1) When did Bleuler first formulate his ideas on 'loosening' of associations, and what influenced him in this regard? 2) Did Bleuler ever meet Janet? Did he have any direct contact with him? 3) How important an influence was Breuer and Freud's 'Preliminary Communication' in 1893 on Bleuler's developing ideas? 4) How much of an influence did Jung's ideas, particularly his 1907 book on Dementia Praecox have on Bleuler? 5) Why was Bleuler so enthusiastic about Freud? 6) How affected was Bleuler and the other Burgholzi physicians by Jung's sojourn with Janet in 1902-1903? 7) When was the term 'schizophrenia' first used around Burgholzi? 8) After Bleuler's book was published in 1911, did Freud read it? 9) Is there any historical record around Manfred Bleuler's invitation to Pierre Janet in 1946 to come to Zurich? Did he feel that Janet was an important influence on his father?

title: Randomised controlled trial of Community Care for People with Schizophrenia in India (COPSI).
description: Study Design: Randomised controlled trial comparing people with schizophrenia allocated to: (i) treatment as usual (TAU), or (ii) TAU and Community Based Intervention (CBI), with 12 month follow-up. Hypotheses: Primary hypothesis: (i) CBI is superior in reducing the symptoms of people with schizophrenia in India compared to TAU, with the primary endpoint at 12 months. Secondary hypotheses: compared with TAU: (ii) CBI is more effective in reducing the disabilities of people with schizophre nia; (iii) CBI is cost-effective; (iv) CBI is more effective in improving the knowledge and attitudes of family members of people with schizophrenia; (v) CBI reduces the impact on care givers; (vi) CBI improves participants adherence to treatment; (vii) CBI reduces participants experience of discrimination. Our ultimate goal is to generate evidence to inform the scaling up of community care for people with schizophrenia in this, and other low resource settings. Setting: Two Indian States : in Tamil Nadu the study will be conducted in rural community clinics; in Goa the study will be conducted in the Institute of Psychiatry and Human Behavior. These sites will improve the generalisability of the findings across different social and care settings, and ensure that recruitment is feasible within the study timeframe.

title: Psychosis and cortico-cortical connectivity.
description: While psychotic disorders are thought to involve a disruption of cortico- cortical connectivity, it is unclear whether this is a correlate of the disorder itself or is related to risk factors for the disorder. This study aims to examine the integrity of cortical connections and the pattern of cortical gyrification in two unique MRI datasets that have been collected over the last five years: one from a large sample of twins discordant for schizophrenia, and another from a cohort of subjects with prodromal signs of psychosis, scanned before and after the onset of the disorder. Both Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) and conventional MRI data have been acquired. Data will be analysed by using a voxel-brain morphometry approach optimized for DTI, DTI tractography and a method for assessing cortical gyrification. The main hypothesis is that abnormal cortical connectivity will be evident in subjects at high risk of psychosis, but to a lesser degree than in patients with psychosis. This study wi ll provide new information on the relationship between cortical gyrification and white matter integrity, and the extent to which abnormalities in these domains underlie the risk of developing psychosis. The findings should inform the development of new interventions aimed at preventing psychosis.

title: A phenomenological study of decision-making capacity in psychiatric disorders.
description: This project will seek to investigate how 3 psychiatric disorders (schizophrenia, severe depression, frontal brain syndrome) threaten capacity to make decisions by probing the task of decision as the patient encounters it(the phenomenology). It will focus on the 'use and weigh' ability for mental capacity used by English law because this is both most relevant for these disorders and also most difficult to interpret. The research builds on a completed cross-sectional study funded by the Wellcome Trust that forms the basis for my PhD in which I conducted capacity assessments using the MacArthurCompetence Assessment Tool on 200 patients admitted to psychiatric hospital and again one month later. This project will use a qualitative design with ethical and phenomenological analysis. In depth interviews will seek to clarify how the 'use and weigh' ability can be threatened by psychiatric disorder. Because mental capacity crosses three disciplines: psychiatry, law and philosophy, this research needs to be interdisciplinary. I will bring Professor Wayne Martin - an expert on theories of autonomy and judgement - into collaboration with these interviews and their analysis. I will also consult closely with Professor Genevra Richardson - an experienced mental health lawyer. I have established working relations with both these academics on mental capacity. The goal of the research is both practical (to inform and improve practical assessments of capacity) and theoretical (to inform and enrich philosophical discussions about autonomy through the study of decision- making inability).

title: Genetic investigation of life course phenotypes of mental health and illness in the 1946 British birth cohort.
description: Using repeated measures collected between ages 13 and 53 years in the British 1946 birth cohort we will test associations between hypothesis-driven candidate genes and novel, empirically derived life-course phenotypes of depression and anxiety, cognition and personality. Our new phenotypes are longitudinal latent classes and latent quantitative traits derived from innovative psychometric approaches that we have piloted (Colman et al, 2007). Goal 1 confirms and 2 extends the phenotypes from m ental health to personality (neuroticism) and cognition ( g ). Goal 3 involves conducting single and multi-marker genetic association studies exploring the impact of sets of genes related to brain development, neurotransmission, cognitive ageing, and endocrine function on these summary measures of life-course risk for health and psychiatric symptoms, personality and cognition. Our overarching hypothesis is that these higher-fidelity, longitudinal measures will represent more valid targets for genetic research than conventional cross-sectional, binary diagnoses. Goal 4 considers the impact of three specified effect modifiers (G x E interaction). These include an early environmental adverse event (childhood separation), pubertal stage (in early teenage years) and a protective factor, educational/occupational attainment. This research will serve as a platform for thematically and methodologically linked collaborative work in other British cohorts, and other relevant samples.

title: Interviews with post-war pioneers in the field of psychiatry, philosophy and anthropology
description: The proposed research will be facilitated by three meetings: (1) with Dr. Jean Oury of La Borde Clinic, (2) with Emeritus Professor Henri Maldiney in Lyon (3) with Professor Levi-Strauss and (4) time permitting, with the poet and novelist Francois Cheng (Officier de la Légion d'honneur Chevalier des Palmes académiques, Commandeur des Arts et des Lettres).

title: PREMIUM: A program for effective mental health interventions in under- resourced health systems
description: The proposed program (?PREMIUM?) aims to define a systematic methodology for the development and evaluation of psychological treatments for delivery by Community and Lay Health Workers and to test this methodology for two mental disorders of global health significance, viz., Depressive Disorder and Alcohol Use Disorders. In the first phase, the program will implement the systematic methodology for development of treatments, derived from three distinct sources of experience and knowledge, to answer two key questions: what are the components of the treatment and how should it be delivered. This phase will comprise a number of sequential steps: synthesis of global and local evidence through systematic reviews and search of the gray literature; determining components of the treatment through consultations with diverse stakeholders; determining an acceptable and feasible delivery model for the treatment through formative research case studies; and testing the intervention in the real world in pilot trials. In the second phase, the clinical and cost- effectiveness of the treatments developed will be evaluated in parallel group randomized controlled trials with primary health care attenders. In the final phase, the findings will be disseminated and a framework for increasing access to these treatments within routine health care programs developed.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: Rationality and Sanity: Implications of a Diagnosis of Mental Illness for Autonomy as Self Governance.
description: First, I intend to explore the relationship between rationality and sanity in the context of the philosophy of psychiatry. Does a diagnosis of mental illness carry a judgement that the person with that mental illness is not rational? Second, I intend to consider some of the ethical implications of judgements of irrationality. Does irrationality entail a failure in the capacity to think and act autonomously and, say, make decisions about one's own treatment? For each of these research objectives, I plan to prepare two publications. I will write an entry about the relationship between rationality and sanity for the Oxford Handbook for the Philosophy of Psychiatry, and a chapter of my monograph on "Irrationality" (Polity Press) will be dedicated to this topic. Moreover, I will prepare one co-authored and one single-authored article on the ethical implications of judgements of irrationality in the context of psychiatry.

title: Complementary studies of learning and motivation in psychosis and pathological hyperphagia.
description: The proposal is based on the hypothesis that psychosis and pathological hyperphagia may be understood in terms of differing perturbations within reinforcement learning circuitry and that parallel explorations of these perturbations will generate complementary insights both to the conditions themselves and to the neurobiology of reward processing generally. The following are the key goals: To conduct parallel clinical and normative studies leading to a detailed understanding of how primary ( food) and secondary (financial) rewards, as well as environmental predictors of those rewards, are associated with deranged (psychosis) or enhanced (MC4R deficiency) motivation and responding. To further our neural understanding of these two serious health problems and, in doing so, enhance knowledge of how and why humans respond to reinforcing stimuli. To gain insights into how reinforcement learning circuitry is integrated with endocrine and metabolic signals, elucidating the ways in whi ch these signals translate into complex behaviours including attention, motivation and learning. To examine general motivational disturbances in psychosis under different circumstances (early onset psychosis, established psychosis, ketamine-induced psychosis) and to extend this to examine food-related motivational changes pertinent to the eating and metabolic changes found in association with schizophrenia and antipsychotic treatment.

title: Medical and Cultural Constructions of Female Mental Illness in Britain and the United States, 1948-1965
description: This dissertation will explore changing conceptions of female depression and anxiety disorders in Britain and the United States to uncover the formative role of different health care systems in the development of psychiatric categories and their popular representation. In doing it will analyse the relationship between internal, national cultures and international cultures within the specific context of postwar gender and medical developments.

title: 'The Eradication of Schizophrenia in Western Lapland' - Research and Development for a new play to tour in 2014.
description: Ridiculusmus is planning an 8-week research and development project in order to create a new play entitled The Eradication of Schizophrenia in Western Lapland. The aim of this project is NOT to create a production, but for Ridiculusmus to engage in scientific research, enquiry and dialogue to gain significant understanding of specific medical specialisms, in order to inform the writing of a new play. We will consult and interact with two molecular psychopharmacologists and psychiatrists, and a clinical psychologist and family therapist to investigate the effects of drugs on dialogue in a therapeutic setting. In particular, we are focusing on the treatment of schizophrenia and anxiety disorders, in order to write a script that is anchored in the reality of contemporary medical practice. Ridiculusmus will undertake workshops, rehearsals, sharings and script development alongside ongoing dialogue and exchanges with medical specialists. This project will enable the company to ga ther the knowledge and material to enable us to create a new theatre production in 2014, which will consequently tour in the UK and abroad, stimulating interest, excitement, learning, thinking and debate around pharmacology and therapeutic dialogue, and an examination of the personal, societal and cultural impacts of current medical practices in relation schizophrenia and anxiety disorders. This project will support a research and development process towards this.

title: Pyschobible: The Book Behind the Battle in Mental Health.
description: The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) is one of the most powerful scientific books of our time: a 1000-page bible for psychiatrists around the world, giving rise to vicious controversies that reflect deep rifts at the heart of the field. This film tells the story of the people and politics behind the DSM, combining interviews with key figures in the book's development and prominent British psychiatrists, stories of patients whose lives have been affected by DSM diagnose s, and archival and creative explorations of mental-illness diagnoses over time to create a unique social history of modern psychiatry.

title: Separation Anxiety and the Making of Animal Psychiatry.
description: My research will demonstrate how, and why, veterinarians and other animal practitioners used human psychiatric diseases as models for animal psychopathology. I will show how animals were perceived to suffer psychopathology outside of the laboratory and explore how this was a consequence of changing attitudes to companion animals, of how the animal mind was understood, and an increasing reliance on brain chemistry. I shall analyse this history with a focus on the condition 'separation anxiety' . John Bowlby developed this theory of attachment partly using animal psychological experiments and replaced emotions with instincts. This allowed the later application directly to animals. My thesis will shed new light on how closely intertwined human and animal psychiatry became in the twentieth-century. There are five main goals to this project: - To address a gap in existing scholarship as no comprehensive study of animal psychiatry exists. - To show how the veterinary profession used human psychiatric disease as a model for animal psychopathology. - To demonstrate the links between the mind and behaviour in twentieth-century Britain. - To explore the changing status of companion animals. - To consider the influence of animals on modern psychiatry.

title: Beyond Diagnosis? Novelty, Need and the Normative in Twenty-First Century Psychiatry.
description: Psychiatric research is today being transformed by new strategic funding initiatives (e.g. from the Wellcome Trust and the US National Institute of Mental Health). Some of these urge scientists to go beyond diagnosis in investigations of mental illness, and move away from diagnostic texts like the World Health Organization's ICD and the controversial US DSM-5. Many studies instead seek to contribute to new classifications of mental disorders, based on biology, and which could enhance innovation in drug discovery. This University Award project seeks to understand the rationales underlying these strategic (and contested) initiatives, their impact on laboratory research, and their effects on how psychiatrists understand and treat their patients. It uses qualitative methods to do so. Broader questions can then be investigated throughout the Award: about the role of science in generating disease constructs; the place of diagnosis in research and practice; the relationships between the labor atory and the clinic; and the ways in which ascriptions of novelty, need and the normative come to shape, direct and propel biomedicine. The project draws on and contributes significantly to STS and medical sociology concepts, generating findings of relevance and import to a range of audiences within and beyond academia.

title: The Temptation of Saint Anthony - psychiatry and religion.
description: 'The Temptation of St. Anthony' is a new devised theatre performance, created by The Mechanical Animal Corporation and presented at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival 2015. It aims to engage public audiences in issues surrounding the significance of religious experience upon biomedical practice. This project responds to recent studies of the impact of 'spirit possession' cases upon psychiatric practice in the UK. Creatively engaging with psychiatric and anthropological analyses of possession state s, 'St. Anthony' asks how physical ensemble performance might provide a fresh, much-needed exploration into the complex nature of possession. To achieve this the creative team (directed by Tom Bailey) collaborates with researchers across the disciplines of Psychiatry (Dr. Simon Dein, Dr. Hugh Grant-Peterkin), Anthropology (Prof. Bettina Schmidt) and Medical Humanities (Dr. Anna Harpin). In a number of UK religious communities possession by a foreign spirit is believed to cause mental illness, requiring religious forms of treatment (such as deliverance or exorcism). For psychiatrists, cases involving possessed patients present a culturally-sensitive interface between clinical medicine and religious healing practices. How to treat mental illnesses embedded within religious contexts? Is there a border between psychiatry and the roles that religious healing practices fulfil? These issues provide a catalyst for a contemporary re- exploration of the legend of 'St. Anthony', depicting a man's epic struggles to maintain both faith and sanity while possessed in the desert. Offering an exciting thematic correlation for our research, the legend provides a compelling narrative framework through which to engage audiences.

title: Necessary Fictions? Text and Response in Depression and Anxiety
description: The project will systematically excavate the interaction between two common mood disorders—anxiety and depression—and narrative fiction. This will be achieved using a three-strand, hybrid framework that blends digital, experimental and interpretive methods derived from computational linguistics, experimental psychology and literary studies. This will impact on the understanding of mood disorders by disclosing how they interact with several key features of narrative (and culture generally). Pratically, the project will analyse the psychological impact of 50k texts from Project Gutenberg using manchine learning. The results of doing this will be experimentally evaluated against subclinical populations, and intepretively evaluated against the experiences of present-day and historical readers using reader panels and reading history databases. At all points, the digital, experimental and intepretive strands will be used to correct and evaluate each other. Theoretical outcomes of the project will involve a deepened understanding of the interaction between literature and mental illness. A practical outcome will be a database of texts that have been rated for therapeutic effect in the treatment of two disorders that affect 1 in 5 people and cost the UK exchequer £25bn annually.

title: CultureClash: When women-of-colour encounter mental health services
description: According to the Mental Health Foundation “African-Caribbean people are more likely to be treated under a section of the Mental Health Act and more likely to receive medication, rather than be offered talking treatments.” For women of colour, rates of mental health problems are higher than average due to “psychological factors that result directly from their experiences, include racism, cultural alienation, and violence and sexual exploitation” - blackwomenshealth.com CultureClash is a research-based and arts-based public engagement project which uses theatre as a launching-off point to ask: How can \- a better understanding of patients’ culture and heritage; \- a better understanding of socio-political contexts of healthcare and background of practitioners; \- better communication between people (particularly women) of colour and mental health professionals improve outcomes for mental health service users. CultureClash brings together researchers, artists, service users and the public to engage in vital and urgent mental health research via 5 outputs: \- artist/scholar research \- live performance \- workshops with service users \- public panel discussions \- symposium for all stakeholders to deliver Wellcome Trust aims of empowering people to engage with health research, making health research more people centred and enabling people to think critically about health research.

title: 4.48 engages the deaf community nationally with mental health debate
description: With the 2018 production nominated for multiple awards, reaching 1, 713 people in person and 11, 808 online, 4.48 will upscale in 2019, actively engaging marginalised deaf communities in four UK localities with new deaf mental health research and debate. The 2018 project broke a significant ‘taboo’ around openly discussing deaf mental health, which affects 50% of the deaf community. Academic involvement revealed widespread ignorance around use of BSL/sign in psychosis, minimal available bilingual support, a need for more deaf-qualified professionals and no recent deaf sector statistics. Delivered with 4 national organisational partners and 4 academic researchers, 4.48 will grow debate and research, with its fulcrum a revival of 4.48 PSYCHOSIS delivered alongside an extended auxiliary event programme. 4.48 will transport deaf mental health debate to locations where it has never been discussed, enabling more extensive deaf engagement and ongoing advocacy. The project’s legacy will be three-fold. New resource materials will be available. A national online network will link all 4 regional communities in advocacy and debate. A combined Vlog from academic researchers will identify recommendations for change around use of sign, regional needs and improvements to bilingual provision, growing awareness of this vital issue in creative and relevant ways.

title: The Vulnerable Self: A Neurophenomenological Model of the Onset of Schizophrenia Spectrum Disorders
description: Research into the schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders faces a number of challenges: the causes of these disorders remain obscure; the field has limited ability to predict which symptomatic young people will progress to diagnosable disorder; and treatments remain unsatisfactory. We argue that progress on these issues can be achieved by renewed focus on “core” trait features of schizophrenia spectrum disorders and improved integration of different domains or levels of analysis (phenotypic, neurobiological, genetic, etc.). The basic self-disturbance model holds significant promise for achieving these aims. Our vision is that by testing and refining this theoretical model in patients in early stages of psychotic disorders we will: significantly advance knowledge of core disturbances and possible aetiological mechanisms underlying schizophrenia spectrum disorders; introduce a unifying principle to integrate different fields of psychosis research; provide a clinical tool to refine risk prediction for psychotic disorders in young people at high risk and predict illness trajectory in those with a first episode of psychosis; and optimise preventative and early treatments for psychotic disorders. Ultimately, this research aims to improve the health care system’s ability to delay or even prevent psychotic disorders, thus reducing their prevalence and impact on individual lives and society.

title: Psychiatric Comorbidity in Autism Spectrum Disorder
description: Autism Spectrum Disorder (autism) is a long-term condition which affects 1-2% of people [1]. People with autism can have difficulties with social skills and communicating with other people, repetitive behaviour and can have a small range of hobbies or interests. It can affect how people perceive the world. Some autistic people see, hear and feel the world differently. More autistic people are being identified, as people become more aware of the condition. Mental health problems are common in autistic people, but we don’t understand why. This project will look at this, and what effects genetics or lifestyle have. We will study the rates of mental health problems in a group of people with autism taken from the National Centre for Mental Health (NCMH) Database, as well as people with autism from two large datasets of anonymised health records. A small number of autistic people with anxiety will then be seen and assessed more deeply. Through this we will assess the effects of genetic risk and life choices on mental health.

title: Strengthening CAre in collaboration with People with lived Experience of psychosis in Uganda (SCAPE-U)
description: We plan to use a pilot cluster randomized controlled trial (RCT) design to assess the feasibility and acceptability of people with lived experience of psychoses participating in multiple levels of the healthcare delivery system (primary care, community, and home) in Uganda. Using process evaluation with both qualitative and quantitative methods, we will yield new information on the benefits and strategies for people with lived experience to meaningfully collaborate across the tiers of healthcare delivery and ultimately transform the continuum of care in low-resource settings. In the longer term, we envision a responsive and capable primary health care service in which patients with psychosis are routinely provided affordable, culturally appropriate and effective psychosocial interventions

title: Targeting sleep to improve anxiety and depression in young people
description: Genetic, epidemiological, and experimental evidence suggests that sleep and circadian rhythm disruption is implicated in the causation of psychiatric disorders. We hypothesise that such disruption influences neurobiological mechanisms that underpin emotion regulation, driving the development and maintenance of anxiety and depression. This research will examine how sleep restriction therapy (SRT), the most effective single component treatment strategy for insomnia, improves mental health. We will perform two randomised controlled trials to test the effects of SRT on sleep physiology, circadian timing, arousal, and neural mechanisms sub-serving emotion regulation. In a third study, we will develop and test an adaptation of SRT - combining it with light therapy - aimed at augmenting depression outcomes. We will recruit young adults because this is the recognised risk period during which symptoms typically incubate, and the time at which early intervention may be most helpful. Our programme of work is informed by lived experience experts, who will be involved in every aspect of the research, and supported by Vocal, an organisation dedicated to inclusive public involvement in health research. Our work will deliver new insights on the link between sleep disruption and mental health, and lead to refinement of sleep intervention for patient benefit.

title: Validation of a translatable chronobiological signature of early relapse in bipolar disorder
description: The aim of this multi-national project is to provide a quantum advance in understanding the mechanisms of sleep and circadian rhythm disruption amongst people with established bipolar disorder (BD). Our methodological focus is a high-resolution signal of specific relevance to BD – the 24-hour rest-activity rhythm as measured by actigraphy. Across four work packages, distinct sleep and circadian features from this signal will be parsed through a machine learning approach called network analysis, and validated as a predictor of early relapse amongst inter-episode patients (Study 1 Australia), as a covariate of recovery from acute manic and depressive illness (Study 2 New Zealand), and as a proxy of endogenous circadian pathogenesis of BD (Study 3 India). In the integrative Work Package 4, findings from these complementary investigations will be cross-validated and synthesised into a theoretically and empirically grounded chronobiological signature of early relapse in BD. This biosignature could be the basis for a future automated early warning technology for BD (our long-term goal). Work Package 4 will also generate a new multi-national dataset and data processing pipelines to be shared with future researchers. Our multi-disciplinary team is uniquely qualified to undertake this project in collaboration with our long-standing lived experience collaborators.

title: Risk stratification for early-onset major depressive disorder
description: The offspring of parents with mental illness represent a major lost opportunity for early-intervention. Having a parent with mental illness is the most common potent risk factor for early-onset depression. Early-onset depression (by age 24) is difficult to treat and is associated with a recurrent/chronic course and poor outcomes. Early-intervention strategies are effective when targeted at this group. However, we know that very few access support. There is also substantial variation in absolute levels of risk meaning that all offspring of parents with mental illness are unlikely to require early-intervention, and service constraints make this infeasible. Early detection and intervention that is personalized dependent on absolute level of risk is therefore needed to improve access to early-intervention for those at ultra-high-risk of developing early-onset depression. We will harness big-data to stratify risk for early-onset depression. We will validate the risk-stratification tool in an independent data set and test response to early-intervention in an already funded trial. Throughout, we will collaborate with lived experience experts and clinicians to ensure the risk-stratification tool is acceptable and develop implementation guidance together. The tool will help to promote timely, personalized access to early intervention for those at ultra-high-risk. Keywords: early-intervention, depression, risk, stratification

title: A Phase II randomised double blind, placebo-controlled trial of oral ketamine as an augmentation treatment for treatment resistant bipolar II depression
description: Our project will conduct the largest phase II randomised clinical trial of ketamine in adults with bipolar depression, to assess the safety and preliminary efficacy of abuse-deterrent oral ketamine in underserved patient population. Bipolar depression II (BD-II), characterized by recurrent episodes of hypomania and depression, is a prevalent subtype of bipolar disorder (BD). Up to 1 of 4 BD-II cases are treatment-resistant (TRBD-II), where prior courses of therapy fail repeatedly. While low doses of the anesthetic ketamine have shown rapid and robust antidepressant effects in adults with TRBD-II, no comprehensive, systematic clinical studies of this intervention have been conducted. Meanwhile, access to intravenous or intranasal ketamine in general is limited by safety, financial and logistical challenges. Given these unmet clinical needs in TRBD-II, Neurocentrx has developed a novel abuse-deterrent capsule formulation of oral ketamine. Our clinical study can confirm whether abuse-deterrent oral ketamine may provide a new effective treatment option for TRBD-II. We will also validate a new clinical care protocol for oral ketamine, where administration starts in clinics and then transitions to home treatment settings. In total, our proposal can help provide a new treatment approach to improve accessibility and expand treatment options for TRBD-II patients.

title: Prisons, Drugs and Mental Health: an interdisciplinary global study
description: We and others have researched colonial and post-colonial criminal justice systems and drugs cultures. However, there remain crucial gaps in knowledge about drugs/addiction in prisons and their relationship to mental health. This is important because evidence suggests that drug laws and enforcement disproportionately affect already marginalised populations, and drug users in prison have poorer health and socio-economic outcomes, but we do not yet fully understand their historical genesis or impacts. Our interdisciplinary programme will research the production, supply, use, and lived experience of drugs among prison communities, c.1800 to the present day. Our team will conduct case study research on former British slave colonies in Guyana, the Caribbean, and Indian Ocean – multi-ethnic societies presenting varied prisons and drugs cultures and mental health challenges. We will also establish and support an international network to research other British, European, and South/Latin American colonies and successor independent polities, extending our global reach through co-production of findings and outputs. Integrating the two components of our programme will produce historicised knowledge, insights, and concepts to address a significant scholarly gap and meet the urgent imperative to reduce long-term health challenges and inequalities associated with drugs and their burden on criminal justice systems globally.

title: MINDCLIMATE: Integrating Mental Health into Climate Change Policy in Zimbabwe: A Multisectoral Approach
description: Our goal is to ensure that Zimbabwe’s climate policy response integrates mental health by generating policy-relevant evidence on links between mental health and climate change and potential policy responses. We hypothesize that chronic and acute climate impacts, mediated through agricultural disruption and food insecurity, contribute to increased anxiety, stress, and depression, but can be mitigated through community-based interventions such as the Friendship Bench. We will combine high-resolution environmental data, historical survey data and a cross-sectional survey in 8 districts complimented by the installation of remote weather monitoring stations to enhance climate data granularity and community knowledge to examine associations between climate variability and mental health outcomes. We will apply human-centered design methods to co-develop community-led adaptation strategies and work with policymakers to translate evidence into climate- resilient mental health policies and integrate mitigation strategies into community platforms such as the Friendship Bench model. Public awareness activities, including multimedia campaigns, will promote climate and mental health literacy at community and national levels. This work will fill critical evidence gaps, inform national climate adaptation planning, and promote inclusive, resilience-building approaches that integrate mental health into Zimbabwe’s broader climate resilience strategies.
recipient: Zvitambo Institute for Maternal and Child Health Research

title: Improving mental health among UK adolescents through a school-based sleep intervention
description: This project will prepare to test the efficacy, cost-effectiveness, and scalable delivery of a sleep intervention to treat adolescent depression and anxiety by building on an established, evidence-based sleep programme, utilising existing school mental health delivery structures, and by strengthening links with implementing partners. The sleep need in young people with mental health problems is high, unmet, and likely to impact on ability to benefit from other interventions. Sleep interventions have proven efficacy to improve symptoms of anxiety and depression alongside broader positive impacts on mental health and functioning. We will address the key knowledge gap of how to implement a sleep intervention across Mental Health Support Teams in Schools (MHSTs) in the UK. We have 3 objectives: 1) To create a sustainable partnership between researchers, stakeholders, and implementation partners. 2) To generate study protocols for the intervention and trial design, as well as co-designing effective recruitment, measurement, and data collection processes. 3) To prepare for a cluster-randomised controlled trial of a Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) programme “The Better Sleep Programme” on depression and anxiety in MHSTs. These foundational activities will establish a sustainable school-based model for improving mental health, designed and fit for future scale-up.

title: Co-Creating and Scaling a Tailored, Lay-Delivered Group Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy (G-CBT) Intervention for Depression Among Young People Living with HIV (YPLHIV) in Cameroon: A Hybrid Implementation-Effectiveness Study
description: This proposal, led by the Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI) Cameroon in collaboration with the National AIDS Control Commission (NACC), the Directorate of Health Promotion, and an association of lived-experience experts, aims to adapt and scale a lay-delivered Group Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy (G-CBT) model to strengthen the management of depression among young people living with HIV (YPLHIV, aged 15–24 years) in Cameroon. The project will unfold in two linked phases. The Foundation Phase will establish coordination structures, assess evidence and site readiness, and co-create and culturally adapt the G-CBT model with youth and lived-experience experts. This phase will culminate in an implementation package—comprising an intervention manual, facilitator training curriculum, supervision and fidelity-monitoring tools, and a finalized protocol to guide the Impact Phase. description: Since its inception in 2009 the World Health Summit (WHS) has become an important platform and convener of diverse stakeholders from all sectors to catalyze better solutions for a healthier world. The WHS’s role is especially important in times of concurrent crises across the globe that affect global health on multiple levels. Over the past years, some cross-cutting themes have emerged as key issues that need to be addressed in this context, among them climate change and health, antimicrobial resistances, mental health, but also diversity, equity, and inclusion. The WHS provides a safe and open space for intersectoral discussions among key stakeholders on these issues through a range of different formats, including the annual main conference in Berlin, the WHS Regional Meeting which is held in various locations around the globe, and smaller by-invitation-only dialogue formats taking place in Berlin and other cities. With the support from partner organizations including the Wellcome Trust, the World Health Summit aims to “bring the right people to the table”, i.e., those who are key to designing and implementing solutions to these critical issues, including people with lived experiences and especially from the global south.

title: SPARK-PMDD: Studying Psychological Changes and Inflammatory Markers in Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD)
description: Background: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) is a severe reproductive mood disorder with distressing symptoms that emerge monthly in the week or two before menstruation. For people with PMDD, cyclical symptoms cause a great deal of difficulties at home, work, and/or school. Previous research from our team has shown elevated inflammatory levels in people with depression and postpartum depression. This study aims to understand whether severity of PMDD symptoms is linked to variation in inflammatory levels across the menstrual cycle. Approach: We will recruit people with and without PMDD and ask them to complete daily questionnaires about their PMDD symptoms, and other psychological processes. Blood samples will be collected at 2 timepoints during their menstrual cycle to measure inflammation levels in their bodies. At these times, participants will also be asked to provide detailed information about thought processes like self-criticism, body image, rumination (repetitive distressing thoughts), and suicidality (thoughts, plans, behaviours related to suicide). Additionally, we will gather participants’ opinions on biological and psychological treatments for PMDD and their lived experiences with the disorder. Impact: There are currently limited available treatments for PMDD. With this data, we will provide a better understanding of ways to improve treatment for this underrecognised disorder.

title: The spectrum of early Tuberculosis treatment responses: evaluating associations with post-treatment outcomes
description: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a significant global health concern with an estimated 1.25 million deaths and 10.8 million incident cases in 2023. Programmatic outcome definitions focus primarily on mortality and cure, rather than long-term wellbeing. Estimates of residual post-TB lung damage range from 18-80%, nutritional recovery post TB is slow and in many cases incomplete, and studies reviewing quality of life, report improvement on treatment but no complete resolution to pre-TB levels. This fellowship aims to improve the understanding of the spectrum of TB severity at presentation and how this relates to treatment response in individuals diagnosed with TB to identify prognostic factors associated with post-TB morbidity and develop a standardised method of TB severity scoring. This will be achieved through a 9-month observational longitudinal cohort study of a people with newly diagnosed TB in Zimbabwe, with close observation of respiratory status, immune activation, nutritional markers, disease burden, and mental health early in disease. Immune activation will be measured through measuring a panel of matrix metalloproteinase levels in plasma and sputum. Outcomes will focus on treatment failure, quality of life, nutritional deficiency and lung damage at 9 months. Key words: Tuberculosis, matrix metalloproteinases (MMP), post-TB morbidity, post-TB lung disease

title: Sensory trauma and the school-to-prison pipeline: Changing health and education trajectories through participatory action research.
description: The school-to-prison pipeline refers to the link between negative school outcomes (e.g. school absence/exclusion) and involvement in the criminal justice system. Neurodivergent children experience school absence, exclusion and imprisonment at disproportionately higher rates–particularly when also racially minoritised or from low-income families. Most exclusions are for “disruptive behaviour”; this focus on risk rather than vulnerability means behaviour is met with exclusion/criminalisation rather than being recognised as an unmet mental health need. However, recent research suggests “challenging behaviour” in neurodivergent populations may be coping mechanisms or responses to sensory stress. Through participatory action research, this study will investigate the role of sensory stress in the school-to-prison pipeline. We will use a range of qualitative and quantitative methods (e.g. interviews, rating scales, heart-rate monitoring, and sound/light level meters) to explore sensory experiences in mainstream school, alternative provision and secure custody settings. We will test whether factors (e.g. classroom behaviour, school avoidance) linked to negative outcomes (e.g. school nonattendance, exclusion, custody) are underpinned by sensory stress and intersecting identity categories. We aim to inform school- and custody-based interventions that promote better mental health, educational and justice outcomes.

title: Mentorship as a Tool for Equity: Strengthening Respectful Clinical and Research Learning Environments in Sierra Leone
description: Sierra Leone has made significant progress in rebuilding its health workforce, yet the clinical learning environment for junior doctors remains fragile. Evidence from the University of Sierra Leone Teaching Hospitals Complex shows that over two-thirds of junior doctors experience academic bullying, including belittling, exclusion, and public humiliation. These behaviours are often normalised as a “rite of passage,” contributing to burnout, psychological distress, and intentions to leave the sector, undermining both workforce retention and patient safety. At the same time, there is strong local appetite for change, with clinicians seeking tools to foster more inclusive culture. This project will co-design, implement, and evaluate an equity-based mentoring programme to address these challenges. Through structured training, coaching, and communities of practice, it aims to disrupt harmful hierarchies, strengthen inclusive leadership, and build psychologically safe clinical and research environments. Co-developed with Sierra Leonean clinicians and led by an interdisciplinary team, the programme aligns closely with Wellcome’s priorities on mental health and equitable research systems. Over 9 months, the project will train 50–60 clinicians, support progression into research and specialist training, and generate robust evidence on impact. Outputs include a mentorship toolkit, evaluation report, academic publications, and a scalable model for national and regional adoption.

title: WHO Global Health Policy and Systems Research Agenda on Disability Health Equity 2026 - 2030
description: The funding proposal focuses on the development of the WHO Global Health Policy and Systems Research Agenda on Disability Health Equity. Overall Goal: The WHO Global Research Agenda will guide research that generates the evidence policymakers need to reduce health inequities experienced by persons with disabilities. Objectives of the Global Research Agenda: 1\. Define the key knowledge gaps and research areas for evidence generation on health equity for persons with disabilities at a global level over the next five years (from 2026 – 2030). 2\. Strengthen knowledge production for evidence-informed policies, plans and practices relating to disability inclusion in health systems strengthening and primary health care. 3\. Build research capacity on health equity for persons with disabilities by creating a framework for research priorities to be applied and further contextualized at the regional and national levels. The Agenda will cut across different areas, such as communicable and noncommunicable diseases, mental health, social determinants of health such as climate, poverty or gender-based violence, and health- systems strengthening, with a strong focus on low- and middle-income countries. It will target Member States; policymakers, national health research bodies and institutes; global research funders; academic institutions; CSOs and NGOs; intergovernmental organizations; and United Nations agencies.

title: An investigation of synaptic transmission between monosynaptically coupled layer III and layer IV neurons and the mechanisms underlying experience- dependent plasticity in the visual cortex.
description: The proposed research will utilize a number of techniques to study the receptor mediated and molecular mechanisms underlying synaptic plasticity and experience-dependent development of monosynaptically coupled Layer III and Layer IV neurons in the rat visual cortex. It is well established that cortical physiology is dramatically altered when sensory experience is disrupted. In the visual cortex the behavioural consequences of such manipulations are particularly apparent due to the fact that they result in vision or blindness. Although much research has been carried out to determine the effects of various types of visual deprivation and experience, very little is known about the synaptic modifications and molecular processes which underlie plasticity in the visual cortex. The synaptic modifications will be investigated using ex vivo slices from animals which have had altered visual experience. Electrophysiological recordings will then be made between Layer III and Layer IV neurons, in vitro, to determine the experience-dependent alterations in synaptic transmission compared to in vitro recordings from animals reared with normal sensory experience. In addition to the electrophysiological recordings, experience-dependent changes in the synaptic architecture and the localization of neurotransmitter receptors will be investigated. After completion of this stage in the work the project with go on to attempt to induce the same modifications in acutely prepared visual cortical slices or in visual cortical cultures to determine the molecular mechanisms involved. The project also provides the opportunity to test the long-standing, but unproven, hypothesis that the mechanisms of long-term potentiation and long-term depression contribute naturally to synaptic modifications.

title: Anglo-Dutch-German Workshop: 'Patients' Body Perceptions.
description: Workshop: Anglo-Dutch-German Workshop on 'Patients' Body Perceptions', University of Warwick, 11-13 July 2003 The workshop is one of a series of workshops organised with colleagues in the Netherlands (Amsterdam/Maastricht) and Germany (Stuttgart) and the Wellcome Centre for the History of Medicine in London. The first of these gatherings, initially co-organised by Dutch and British scholars, took place in Amsterdam in 1997 and in 2000 we were joined by a group of German colleagues, forming an Anglo-Dutch-German collaboration. Topics covered in previous workshops include neurasthenia, social psychiatry, the patient in history, and cultures of medicine. For the 2003 workshop we have decided to include the early modern period, to strive for a more ambitious approach to the theme, and to develop comparisons over time as well as between countries. The workshops have urged the participation of established scholars as well as younger colleagues, including graduate students. The workshop is organised around pre-circulated papers and invited commentaries. This formula has worked well in the past, encouraging engagement with the papers, and assisting us to proceed rapidly to publication. The volume based on the 1999 Warwick conference is in press (due 2002). A further volume is planned based on the 2003 workshop.

title: Protein kinase C involvement in u-opioid receptor desensitization and morphine tolerance.
description: Opioid drugs such as morphine produce their therapeutic effects (e.g. analgesia) and unwanted effects (e.g. euphoria and respiratory depression) by acting at the m-opioid receptor (MOR). In the whole animal tolerance develops rapidly to the effects of morphine, even after a single dose. It had been assumed that receptor desensitization was a fundamental component of opioid tolerance. However, morphine, unlike other MOR agonists, does not produce rapid MOR desensitization. This has led to the suggestion that morphine produces tolerance precisely because it does not induce rapid receptor desensitization, but rather because it continues to activate the receptors thus evoking other adaptive changes in the cell that result in the development of tolerance. We, on the other hand, have recently discovered that in mature brain neurones morphine does produce MOR desensitization but only when protein kinase C (PKC) is activated. Thus crosstalk between Gq-coupled receptors that activate PKC and MORs may play a crucial role in MOR desensitization and this potentially may be an important component in the development and maintenance of morphine tolerance. What now needs to be elucidated is:-1. how PKC activation converts morphine into a rapid, receptor desensitizing agonist. 2. whether PKC/morphine-induced MOR desensitization is responsible for the cellular tolerance that develops in neurones on prolonged morphine exposure In this proposal we describe experiments that are designed to address these issues. The experimental approach will be to study MORs endogenously expressed in mature brain neurones. This is important because different cell types (e.g. neurones vs recombinant expression systems) may differentially express the signalling components required for the development of MOR desensitization and morphine tolerance. Furthermore, it is now imperative to confirm and extend theories on morphine tolerance generated from experiments on recombinant systems to mature neurones because it is in such neurones that tolerance and physical dependence actually occur in the intact animal

title: The emergence of ADHD in European countries: a historical study of child behavioural disorders diagnostic categories from 1950 to 2000.
description: The emergence of ADHD in European countries: a historical study of child behavioural disorders diagnostic categories from 1950 to 2000 This study aims at reconstructing the history of the changes in the medical and psychological conceptualisation and treatment of child behavioural disorders in Great Britain, France, the Netherlands and Italy from 1945 onwards. A special emphasis will be given to the influence of genetic studies and pharmacological remedies on the theory and practice of child psychiatry and psychology. The questions that this research sets out to answer are: How have psychological and biological theories on behavioural disorders among children been interacting over the past fifty years? How did psychopharmacology and neurobiological research change the theory and the practice of child psychiatric and psychological expertise? How did the above-mentioned change influence the public debate and lay perception of child disorders? The proposed research is an extension of my previous study on the history of child behavioural disorders in France, Britain and Italy (But Fidgety Phil/He Won't Sit Still From Instability to Hyperactivity, c.1890s-1990s, PhD. Thesis, University of Amsterdam, June 2001). I plan to study the developments in the psychiatric debate in Italian, British, French and Dutch medical journals, textbooks of child psychiatry and monographies devoted to child behavioural disorders. In addition, I plan to extend my research to the information channels through which medical professionals or other groups (such as parents' associations and pharmaceutical companies) disseminate information about child behavioural disorders among lay people.

title: Clinical Research Facility at Hammersmith Hospital: Equipment Award.
description: The Hammersmith Hospital, an integral part of Imperial College London and home to the MRC Clinical Sciences Centre, has witnessed a substantial expansion of both basic science resources and clinical service over the past few years. Imperial College is now co-ordinating a further £160M renovation to develop Hammersmith Hospital as its principal centre for clinical research. Already under construction is a large research block that will house the GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) Clinical Imaging Centre and Imperial College neurosciences laboratories. The GSK investment is the largest by a pharmaceutical company in an academic site and will be operational by Q4 2006. A new building on what is currently 'J' block at Hammersmith will accommodate the move of the Kennedy Institute of Rheumatology from Charing Cross Hospital by 2009. A third new building, to replace adjacent 'L' block, will bring together genomic medicine, vascular inflammation and immunology. Imperial College will invest £25M in a Drug Discovery Institute to bring together clinical scientists, medicinal chemists and biotechnologists in the College to develop in-house products through early phase clinical trials. A redesigned and renovated Wolfson Conference Centre will provide a modern and well- equipped education resource for graduate and post-graduate training. These investments coincide with the focusing of clinical service for neuroscience and psychiatry, cancer, rheumatology and renal medicine at Hammersmith.

title: Transnational migration in SE Asia and the health of children left behind.
description: This project will examine health and welfare outcomes, in four South-East Asian countries, for children under 12 years of age left behind when their father and/or mother became a transnational migrant. Primary cross-sectional data will be collected from both migrant and non-migrant households across sampled communities and will include anthropometric measurements, validated health measures (e.g SDQ) and well-being measures. Multivariate techniques (logistic or multinomial regression) will be used to build a series of models incorporating contextual and individual independent variables and designed to test five important hypotheses. In sum, these formalize expectations that the health and well-being of left-behind children is positively associated with father's absence, and (for physical health) with mother's absence under certain conditions, but (for mental health/well-being) negatively associated with mother's absence. Child age and gender and country/local community characteristics are expected to influence outcomes, once other independent variables are taken into account.Selected qualitative interviews will provide in-depth insight into issues raised and aid the interpretation of quantitative findings. Our key goals are to: 1) establish systematic associations between parental absence and child health/well-being; 2) provide a basis for future longitudinal analysis on an under-researched topic; 3) contribute to an evidence base for policy development.

title: MA History of Medicine.
description: For my MA dissertation I propose to investigate how forensic medicine in Britain in the period between 1829 and 1985 has been able to discover the identity of 1) unidentified corpses in cases of murder, accident or suicide; found either intact or in pieces; and 2) living subjects over whose identity questions have been raised, including missing persons, fraud cases, and unknown amnesia cases. This project is not concerned with the identification of criminals who were still at large - much work has been done on the subject of the use of newly developed techniques in criminal investigations of the nineteenth and twentieth century. I am concerned more with the role of forensic specialists using the unknown body to identify an individual, rather than the use of evidence from the scene of the crime to identify an unknown assailant, or to identify a suspect for an investigation. At the most basic level, I am interested in investigating how forensic specialists 'put names to faces'. The project will address the period between the formation of the Metropolitan Police; and the development of DNA analysis in the process of identification. While undoubtedly the most reliable and successful identification technique, I view DNA analysis as a dependence on chemical science, rather than the analytical skills of the specialist and the detective skills of the police- I am more interested in how several different branches of forensic medicine interacted

title: In Pursuit of the Nazi Mind: The Deployment and Development of Psychoanalysis in the Allied Struggle against Germany.
description: 'In Pursuit of the Nazi Mind' demonstrates how models of the unconscious and cognate clinical techniques contributed to and were reshaped by the Allied struggle against the Third Reich. Important studies of Nazi psychology, centred on the concept of the superego, were mobilised in military intelligence, post-war planning and policy recommendations. My goal is to contextualise and critically assess medico-psychiatric and psychoanalytical endeavours to grasp the irrational wellsprings of N azism, and to show their significance more widely for the history of psychology in western culture. A panoramic survey will cover the emergence of new Freudian approaches to politics in the 1920s, their apotheosis in the 1940s and disintegration in and beyond the 1960s. Five accompanying core cases, for which extensive documentation exists, are designed to illustrate the varied roles and influences of applied psychoanalysis around the war: 1. Testimony of Hess s doctors, in Britain 1941-45, an d at Nuremberg. 2. Studies of Hitler, commissioned by the US Office of Strategic Services in 1941. 3. Experiments conducted upon Nazi sympathisers through the Allied Control Commission, 1945-6. 4. Psychoanalytic materials furnished to the UNESCO project, Tensions Affecting International Understanding' , 1947-51. 5. Clinical evaluations of imprisoned Nazi murderers psychic lives, 1945-1970.

title: The Reluctant Visionaries.
description: Our documentary will investigate the phenomena of visions, hallucinations and visual disturbances which can be traced to biological causes associated with eye disease. Charles Bonnet Syndrome was first identified 200 years ago but is still largely unrecognized by physicians. Millions of people around the world suffer from it ? yet many keep it secret, fearing they are mentally ill. Our film explores a condition which has a very rational root in certain cases of eye damage and macular degeneration but has led to misdiagnosis of psychiatric illness and may be responsible for some reports of phenomena like ghosts and fairies

title: 'The great class which lies between': Provision for the non-pauper insane in Ireland, 1830-1900.
description: Through a close survey of the records of selected private and district asylums, Commission of Lunacy reports, and official records, the project will explore the domestic and institutional provision for the Irish non-pauper insane from c.1830 to 1900, a period marked by significant socioeconomic change. It will assess whether the emergence of a strong middle-class in this period informed interactions between gender, religion, identity, and insanity, and question whether underlying medical, legal and lay explanations of mental illness and its predisposing factors in this group differed from those attributed to pauper patients in Ireland. The project will reflect on the anxieties that were prompted among local and national authorities, the medical profession and families, inside and outside the asylum, while devising management strategies. It will then assess the impact of these strategies upon patient and family experiences of insanity. This project will consider whether some Irish asylums operated as a mixed economy' of care and will explore how class and religious divisions were played out among the patient and staff populations within the asylums thereby contributing to emerging debates on presence of emotional communities' within asylums. The main outputs comprise a PhD thesis, three articles two policy-related and a workshop.

title: O - The History of Orgasm 3*60' for BBC2/4.
description: This grant is to fund development for a three part television series about the history of the female orgasm. This series is a journey to one of the most complex and misunderstood of human behaviours - the female orgasm. In the company of Dr Alice Roberts we cross millennia and continents, spanning physiology, anatomy and psychiatry, meeting quacks and scientific pioneers, uncovering our most intimate secrets. Ultimately we discover how medicine and science have shaped women's sexuality. This series would ideally coincide with the forthcoming Hollywood movie, Hysteria, scheduled for release in late 2011 starring Maggie Gyllenhaal and Hugh Dancy.

title: Social welfare and public health: analysing quasi-natural experiments from the 2007 recession.
description: Advanced industrialised countries are experiencing social and economic disruption on a scale not seen since World War II. The current economic crisis is leading governments to challenge the assumptions that have underpinned the post-war welfare state. Indeed, some commentators point to social welfare as the cause of economic decline. And, since economic growth leads to better health, they argue continued high levels of investment are a reason for slowing progress in population health. Yet an alt ernative body of research suggests that social welfare can be productive as well as protective. Investing in welfare, it is argued, can be as important, if not moreso, than healthcare and economic growth in improving population health. Empirical data and analysis are crucially needed to understand the relationship between social welfare and population health. Our initial work has pinpointed active labour market programmes as one key policy intervention that can mitigate the mental health risks o f unemployment. The current proposal extends this work to understand: How do social protection programmes affect public health? Which specific welfare investments are the most effective, and what are their mechanisms of effect? Using innovative multi-level quantitative models, we will link existing secondary data sources spanning individual and society levels which have great potential to yield such understanding, but have yet to be used for this purpose across 27 EU countries and over time. The se statistical analyses will address the most important political questions of our time: what is the role of the state in protecting people and public health?

title: The Artful Experts Season.
description: Artful Experts Season is a pilot public engagement programme of exhibitions, music, events and live performances by people with lived experience of mental distress. Curated by arts and mental health charity DLL, the programme will bring together expert collaborators from the fields of mental health, digital media and the arts to explore methods of public engagement, with a view to a larger scale World Mental Health Day 2015 programme. Our Steering Group, Advisory Panel and Creative Collaborato r team will work with an external Evaluator to direct and shape public engagement, evaluative and data gathering methodology; test and critique processes during the programme; and develop material into assets that can inform future public engagement methodology. A two-minute film and formal Evaluation document will be publically shared. Public engagement will be driven by accessible exhibitions and live shows, social media and web activity, including an online animated serial narrated by comic character Dr Bobby. The vibrant programme will culminate in the Artful Symposium. This unusual artist-led event at the Royal Society of Medicine will present invited mental health audiences with art and performances by people with personal experience of mental illness. The aim is that this unique context of a shared mediating experience of art will form the basis for reflection and fresh dialogue around mental health in this historically fraught and polarised field. DLL believes that art can off er a transformative basis for public engagement with mental health, where experts by experience work together with experts by profession.

title: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder in Adults: Use of Eye-Tracker to Detect Attention Deficits
description: Current diagnosis of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) in adults is by subjective measures. Our project examines the value of diagnosis of adult ADHD by objective means through the use of an eye-tracking device. Therefore our proposed goals are: 1\. To find out the prevalence of ADHD using subjective tests in those adults who attend the mental health services in Sligo/Leitrim County, Republic of Ireland2. To investigate the use of an objective test in the diagnosis of ADHD 3. To explore the use of the objective test to distinguish ADHD from its associated comorbid conditions. 4. The results will be disseminated through peer-review publications and at international and national conferences, but most importantly will lead to further studies in which interventions will be tested for their potential to enhance care, and reduce the levels of educational and employments dysfunction of people with adult ADHD symptomatology.

title: An Analysis of Health Behaviour Modifications in Alleviating Fear of Cancer Recurrence (FCR)
description: Cancer afflicts a considerable number of people and may have significant impact on them, such as heart problems and infertility. Distressful emotions, including loneliness and Fear of Cancer Recurrence (FCR) might be experienced. FCR is extrememly common among cancer survivors to varying degrees. In addition, high levels have been associated with depression, hopelessness and other undesirable consequences . As a highly prevalent unmet need of cancer survivors, such implications on their quality of life reveal the importance of research into FCR to improve care for cancer survivors. This research project aims to further investigate the relationship between loneliness, distress and FCR. In particular, it also seeks to study whether modifications in health behaviours can alleviate FCR. Research suggests that diet and physical activity may be key factors in reducing cancer risk. Furthermore, it is thought that FCR might motivate health behavior modifications in cancer survivors. However, more research is needed to delineate this relationship. Moreover, a theoretical understanding of if and how changing health behaviours may help the survivors manage their fears is not available. Therefore, the project will explore the relations between health behaviour modifications and FCR through interviews and surveys to attain both qualitative and quantitative data.

title: Wellcome Centre for Human Neuroimaging
description: Our vision is to deliver clinically-transformative applications of neuroimaging that provide computationally-derived biomarkers for personalised prognosis and treatment planning. We investigate how the human brain functions in health and disease and how this knowledge can inform prognoses in patients with neurological and psychiatric disorders. By integrating cutting-edge neuroimaging technologies with neuronal and behavioural modelling, we seek to establish non-invasive quantitative measures of neuronal function that can be used to identify pathophysiology, deliver personalised prognoses, and develop or assess therapeutic interventions. Our strategy combines two key elements that are unique to our location, staff and facilities. First, we bring together internationally-renowned expertise in neuroimaging, biophysical modelling, cognitive, computational, mathematical and clinical neuroscience. Second, we create an environment that fosters interactions between those asking key neurobiological questions and those developing methods and theories that make these questions tractable. Our clinical focus reflects a long- standing commitment to developing neuroimaging methods that provide mechanistic explanations of how the human brain supports sensory, motor and cognitive functions in health, how these mechanisms are affected by disease, and how they respond to therapeutic interventions. We are in a unique position to conduct this work given our our location opposite the National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery.

title: MA History – Medical Pathway
description: Life in Glamorgan County Lunatic Asylum 1864–1914. Research Problem: To investigate the interaction between the perspectives, practices and responses of professional staff and incarcerated patients within the Glamorgan asylum, in order both to recover the silent voice and lived experience of patients and to reveal the implementation of professional medical theories within the daily life of the asylum itself. Key Goals: To use the archival records of an individual asylum (Glamorgan County Lunatic Asylum) to ask wider questions and challenge traditional generalised narratives of asylum history. \- To exploit the archival asylum records in new and dynamic ways in order to recover the ‘patient voice’ and understand patients as active agents in their asylum patient experience. \- To consider interactions between professional staff and patients in the interpretation of the relationship between the body and the mind within the asylum \- To investigate how physical ‘symptoms’ were used to demonstrate mental illness, and the use of photography in casebooks to consider the idea that madness had a ’face’

title: (MJur) Masters by Research
description: This research will investigate and re-evaluate the dominant features of the ethics of care in application to the legal, ethical and health implications of assisted dying. The application of a care-based ethic will discuss society’s perception of death and define the often ambiguous concept of dying with dignity. This thesis will assess whether a gender-neutral examination of the inter-relational elements of a care-based ethic can be utilised as an alternative to the rights-based analysis found in discourse concerning assisted dying. Further, the assisted suicide debate is particularly important as it incorporates a wide range of ethically significant factors; of which autonomy is a representative example. In addition, the concept and definition of dignity will be examined due to the relative underdevelopment as a concept within Bioethics which is utilised in an unreflective way in the assisted suicide debate. To demonstrate this, cases concerning both the incompetent and competent patient will be evaluated with recourse to the The Suicide Act 1961 Lord Falconer’s Assisted Dying Bill (No 2) and the Director of Prosecutions Guidelines. This research will demonstrate why the community, as family, friends, healthcare professionals and judiciary should be sensitive and receptive to this.

title: Exploring women's health using radio as a tool
description: The project is split in two parts: Part 1 – Working with BME women who have faced or are still facing mental health issues in their lives, caused by drugs, abuse, trauma and social migration. The project will tell the stories of five women covering domestic abuse, substance abuse, ADHD, Social migration and schizophrenia The project will take place between 4Wings and two universities in a relaxed and holistic setting. 4Wings is a women's charity with a focus on abuse and trauma. I have attended sessions with the women in question and they are very open within that setting. Through the support of BBC World Service, UNESCO, British Council, the radio packages will reach a large international audience, building a global community through radio, tackling issues and raising awareness. Part 2 – The radio packages will be played out on BBC Radio Merseyside and iWoman Radio an online global station aimed at women over 25, the content will be used to launch iWoman radio in 2017. Audiences will be able to have a deeper understanding of the different issues the women have gone through but through science.

title: Hiding in Plain Sight. Cultures of Harm in Residential Institutions for Long- Term Adult Care, Britain 1945 to 1980s
description: During the 1970s and early ‘80s, 18 major investigations were conducted into abuse and neglect in long-stay psychiatric hospitals. These inquiries focused primarily on administrative and management failures, giving little attention to the underlying values and belief systems – staff attitudes to pain, suffering, institutionalisation and care – that gave rise to abusive practices, or to the language and behaviours that perpetuated them. In this project, I will return to the extensive documentation generated by two of these inquiries, together with other sources, and ask new and different questions to gain deeper insights into the underlying factors that gave rise to institutional abuse in order to help prevent it in the future. Through a number of publications (one monograph and at least two research-based journal articles) as well as workshops the project will provide current inquiries, policy-makers, health workers and clinicians, and social scientists with valuable historical context around abuse, whilst introducing a new strand of inquiry into historical scholarship.
