Engagement with the wider public is vital for a project such as this and I will regularly contribute opinion pieces for the wider media (newspapers, blogs, public talks, radio), and write at least one theatre or radio play.

title: Improving self-awareness: Manipulating the neural substrates of self-belief
description: Beliefs about our skills and abilities (known as “self-beliefs”) may become divorced from reality, particularly in psychiatric and neurological disorders. For instance, someone with depression may think they are unable to succeed in new pursuits, making them unlikely to try in the first place. My goal is to identify core brain processes supporting self-beliefs, and in turn leverage this knowledge to develop interventions for restoring aberrant self-belief. I will focus on a network of brain regions in medial and lateral prefrontal cortex that is theorized to support estimates of self-ability. I will address three interlocking questions: 1) How are self-beliefs constructed? 2) Which factors permit the modification of self-belief? 3) How are self-beliefs used in the control of future behaviour? I will conduct fMRI and MEG experiments using novel decision paradigms to dissect elements of self-belief computation such as prior experience and task difficulty, and reveal how mental health is linked to these computations through large-scale online data collection. This work will inform behavioural and neurofeedback interventions to modify self- belief. The overarching goal of my research agenda is to produce a comprehensive, mechanistic account of self-belief construction, thereby informing efforts to restore appropriate self-awareness in disorders of mental health.

title: The Same Road is a Different Road
description: The Same Road is a Different Road project will see the creation of installation film piece about a ten-minute walk made in collaboration with marginalised teenage boys in London and Oxford, involved in gang related violence as both perpetrator and victim. Long-term exposure to violence is associated with psychological problems, often undiagnosed. Young people living with constant exposure to violence are at increased risk of a range of mental health conditions including conduct disorder, antisocial personality disorder, anxiety, psychosis and drug and alcohol dependence. The project will enable a collaboration with three neuroscientists as action research, enabling the work, the participating young people and the viewers of the work to engage in the scientific consideration of the development of young peoples’ brains and the potential impact this constant engagement in and exposure to violence has on the increased risk of a range of mental health and psychological conditions that are associated gang related violence. The final work will be exhibited at Modern Art Oxford, enabling viewers to have an insight and understanding of the value of people engaging directly in health research and the impact that it can have on their thoughts, feelings and behaviours.

title: The Synaptic Organisation of the Hippocampus : VTA loop
description: When making decisions, it is advantageous to use past experience to help choose the best option. For example, when deciding whether to drink a strong coffee late in the evening, it is beneficial to weigh up what happened when you drank some previously: that coffee increased your alertness to help you get through that last hour or work; but also that you struggled to sleep later in the day. These kinds of decisions are thought to be determined by the activity of distinct populations of neurons. An example of this are neurons in the hippocampus and ventral tegmental area (VTA), which together have been suggested to form predictions about the results of our decisions. If this is the case, it would be extremely important, as problems in these processes result in an enormous variety of disorders including depression, anxiety and drug abuse. However, because these two areas are connected by very complex circuitry, it has been difficult to find out how they carry out their role. In this proposal our goal is to understand how the neurons in the hippocampus and VTA work together to make these decisions, so we can work out how they go wrong and cause disease.

title: The effects of anti-inflammatory drugs on emotional and reward processing
description: The purpose of these studies is to investigate whether anti-inflammatory drugs change how the brain deals with emotional and rewarding information, with a view to improve treatments for people suffering from depression. There is growing scientific evidence that some people who do not respond to conventional antidepressants may benefit from taking anti-inflammatory drugs. Our research has previously shown that antidepressants affect how people experience certain kinds of information, for example by making them focus on positive facial expressions more than negative ones. These effects on ‘emotional processing’ can be found very early on in treatment, even before a patient ‘feels better’; however, we can measure these early changes and use this information to predict whether the treatment will actually help people feel better in the long term. The drugs we are investigating are called tofacitinib and atorvastatin. These are licensed drugs which has been shown to be generally safe and well-tolerated. We will test whether tofacitinib and atorvastatin can alter emotional processing in the same way as standard antidepressant drugs, comparing them with placebo (dummy tablet). Since reward processing and inflammation have been linked to depression, we will assess the effects of these drugs on these measures too.

title: Neural Simulation as a Neurocomputational Mechanism Underpinning Pathological Worry
description: Worry is the cardinal symptom of generalised anxiety disorder, which affects 6% of the population at any time. Worry may arise from altered functioning of the neurocomputational processes that simulate the future to adaptively avoid danger. My goals are to 1) characterise the neurocomputational processes that use “simulation” to enable avoidance, and 2) determine how changes in these processes are linked to pathological worry. I will use computational modelling, combined with neuroimaging, to reveal how simulations, supported by neural state reactivation, are used to guide decision-making in gamified avoidance tasks. Using state-of-the-art transcranial ultrasound stimulation and pharmacological manipulation, I will determine the causal role of neural circuits and their reliance on core neuromodulators. Finally, I will investigate the origins of aberrant simulation strategies, determining the influence of genetic risk and early-life stress, and testing the influence of real-world stress in adulthood. Later, I will link simulation processes to clinically significant worry, both in the lab and the real world, and investigate how to train more positive simulation strategies. Together, this work will provide insights into the processes supporting avoidance of danger, and indicate how these processes underpin pathological worry. Ultimately, these findings could inform the development of more targeted treatments.

title: Moral terrains: An Anthropology of Green Social Prescribing
description: This is an anthropological investigation of the moral terrains navigated by those engaged in Green Social Prescribing in the UK. Green Social Prescribing is a new government initiative intended to tackle health inequalities and improve mental wellbeing while simultaneously alleviating the need-supply shortfall in NHS mental health provision. Green Social Prescribing involves referring people into voluntary sector organisations that engage with nature, including city farms and gardening groups. My research uses 13 months of ethnographic fieldwork and two rounds of semi-structured interviews to investigate the moral experience of being prescribed access to nature and the moral challenges involved in delivering this form of care. This research attends to staff and service users' perspectives and explores Green Social Prescribing as a site of multiple and sometimes conflicting moral values. It investigates how the ideals of connecting well with nature, and connecting well with others, interact with biomedical sensibilities. It considers how responsibilities and obligations are distributed, negotiated and experienced. Finally, it investigates the impact of particular environments on the moral relationships formed within them. This research is ground-breaking, in that it initiates a new trajectory for medical anthropology, investigating the role morality plays in mediating relationships between nature and health.

title: Characterising the clinical heterogeneity and aetiology of Avoidant Restrictive Food Intake Disorder
description: Avoidant Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID), introduced to the DSM-5 diagnostic classification system in 2013, is a severe feeding and eating disorder marked by food avoidance and restricted intake, with a prevalence of 1-2%, and serious consequences which can include malnutrition, psychosocial distress and in-patient ward tube feeding. ARFID is heterogeneous in clinical presentation, encompassing symptoms such as diminished appetite, sensory-based food aversion, and fear of adverse consequences associated with eating. This heterogeneity has raised important and related questions about the conceptualisation of ARFID. 1\. Should ARFID be conceptualised as either a neurodevelopmental condition, an anxiety disorder, a consequence of metabolic imbalance or a combination of these? 2\. Does ARFID consist of a collection of aetiologically distinct subtypes which will require different treatment approaches? To address this, I will use large-scale cohorts to: 1\. Characterise the heterogeneity of ARFID 2\. Derive data-driven subtypes 3\. Investigate aetiology, and whether subtypes can be aetiologically distinguished With ARFID research in its infancy, now is the time to answer these fundamental questions to inform future aetiological research and intervention approaches. I will work with individuals living with ARFID, services, and the charity Beat, throughout the fellowship to co-produce evidence-based resources, and influence service development.

title: Sensitising brain MRI to cell type and shape
description: We propose to sensitise brain MRI to cell type numbers, shapes, and connectivity. The goal in each case is to achieve cell specificity. We will do so by (1) developing novel molecular MRI contrasts that provide cell or molecule specific signatures read out through the widely used BOLD signal, by (2) enhancing diffusion MRS to provide tissue microstructure intracellularly to distinguish between neuronal, astrocyte, and microglia morphology, and by (3) combining high resolution diffusion and quantitative MRI with 2D and 3D histology and transcriptomics to generate models that can predict cell distribution and optimise mesoscopic brain connectivity. At the end of the eight year project we will have significantly advanced our ability to use MRI as a cell-specific readout of brain architecture and provided key insights into how variation in the cellular architecture of the brain leads to variation in risk and resilience in mental health.

title: The Neurocognitive Mechanisms of Repetitive Negative Thoughts
description: Repetitive negative thoughts (RNTs) are a risk factor for the development and maintenance of anxiety and depression and are the target of treatments for these disorders. The neurocognitive mechanisms that produce RNTs are not well understood. While a number of processes have been associated with them it is not clear: 1\. Whether the identified neural systems are necessary to perform the cognitive computations associated with RNT 2\. Whether changes in the neurocognitive computations are sufficient to produce meaningful changes in RNT This application will address these questions for three candidate neurocognitive processes; the ability to adapt learning to volatility, the tendency to develop habits, the expression of automatic avoidance tendencies. A series of experimental studies will be conducted in non-clinical human participants, including those selected to have higher levels of RNT. Neurocognitive processes will be modulated using transcranial ultrasound stimulation, transcranial magnetic stimulation, pupil-based biofeedback and a cognitive training intervention. Behavioural, neuroimaging, cognitive and symptomatic outcomes will be analysed using reinforcement learning models. The translational role of these processes will be tested in a larger study. Educational and best practice resources will be co-produced with PPIEP members. This application will provide evidence of the causal neurocognitive mechanisms of RNTs.

title: ASCEND-HD: Advancing Support and Care for Emotional Needs and Distress in Huntington's Disease
description: Huntington’s disease (HD) is a neurodegenerative, inherited condition with typical onset between 30-50 years. It causes physical, cognitive and emotional deterioration, and premature death. UK HD prevalence has doubled since 1990, with 8,000 people affected and 32,000 at risk. Worldwide, HD affects five people per 100,000. HD severely impacts mental wellbeing, including depression, anxiety, and suicidality. However, these difficulties are inadequately understood, affected individuals and families struggle to access informed, effective mental healthcare, and routes to meaningful systemic change are lacking. As an HD-specialist clinical psychologist and researcher, with lived experience of HD myself, I am uniquely placed to change this. I will lead ASCEND-HD, a transformative multi-methods programme of much-needed discovery research employing a Theory of Change model and co-production with experts by experience. Combining well-established and highly-novel methods, we will develop comprehensive understandings of how HD affects wellbeing of individuals and families, and of barriers and facilitators to a step-change in HD wellbeing support. I will then co-produce novel evidence-based guidance and resources for understanding mental wellbeing and support needs among HD families. Working with research, clinical and third-sector networks, these transformative tools will shape future interdisciplinary HD wellbeing research internationally, informing innovative new research and real-world change.

title: Functional analysis of the endoplasmic reticulum stress response pathways in C. elegans.
description: Cellular adaptation to an increase in secretory protein flux or to the accumulation of unfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a universally conserved phenomenon in eukaryotes. The complexity of this response however seems to increase considerably when unicellular eukaryotes such as Saccharomyces cerevisiae are compared to multicellular eukaryotes such as humans and mice. The reasons for this are at present unclear but most likely relate to variations in demand for secretory protein biogenesis within specific tissues or at the different developmental stages of metazoans. Studying the multiplicity of the ER protein folding stress responses in metazoans compared to yeast is at present limited. While mammalian and murine tissue specific cell lines can be examined, and transgenic mice engineered, it is extremely difficult to study the changing biosynthetic capacity of cells, modulated by ER stress response pathways, in an entire organism in vivo or to the same molecular depth as in S. cerevisiae. To overcome this problem I intend to use Caenorhabditis elegans, a small nematode worm, as a whole metazoan model in which to study the ER stress response at different developmental stages and within different tissues. By utilising the powerful genetic approaches available in C.elegans and its status as a valuable metazoan model system, it could easily overtake the current mammalian model systems in allowing the dissection of the metazoan secretory pathway. The first stage of the project will be to develop a reporter system for monitoring the ER stress response and relative expression levels of ER stress response genes in C.elegans using the green fluorescent protein (GFP). GFP will be placed under the regulatory control of promoter regions from genes in C.elegans whose homologues in yeast and mammals have been shown to be strongly unregulated upon the accumulation of unfolded proteins in the ER, e.g. KAR2/BiP and LHS1/GRP170 molecular chaperones of the ER. Once created, these reporter constructs will be used to produce transgenic strains of C.elegans and GFP expression examined in all tissues and developmental stages of C.elegans. Both temporal and tissue specific differences in expression may be anticipated with differing secretory pathway load, e.g. elevation in the cells of the cuticle as it is remodelled and expanded at different developmental stages or within the digestive tract as a constant flow of digestive enzymes are released. This will therefore allow the first ever whole organism assessment of ER chaperone requirement, and thus protein processing capacity/load. Induction of the ER stress response over and above that observed in wild type cells can also be used as a direct indicator for both defects in ER protein biogenesis and changing demands for processing capacity. For example mutations in components of the ER processing machinery themselves or treatments with drugs such as tunicamycin, an inhibitor of N-linked glycosylation, have been shown to elicit an ER stress response. Any mutation or elicitor that leads to the accumulation of incorrectly processed proteins in the ER would be anticipated to result in the induction of the ER stress response. Therefore, by combining the GFP reporter strains in C.elegans with the simple yet powerful genetic manipulations possible in this organism, it should be possible to identify components key to the efficient functioning of the metazoan ER and the ER stress response itself. Such a system will be invaluable in dissecting the complexity of the ER stress response in metazoans, providing both tissue specific and temporal information as to when and where a given component is required for normal ER function.

title: Uncovering mechanisms of cellular survival during ER stress.
description: Most proteins destined for secretion or insertion into a lipid membrane undergo folding and post-translational modifications in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). This process is perturbed in a number of important pathological conditions. For example, in the liver of some individuals homozygous for the "Z-allele" of a1-antitrypsin aggregates of the mutant protein accumulate in the ER leading to hepatic damage and decreased secretion of this serum protein, which, in turn, results in emphysema. The capacity of the ER to fold client proteins is maintained in equilibrium with the load on the organelle by several intracellular signaling pathways that are collectively referred to as the Unfolded Protein Response (UPR). These pathways defend the cell against ER stress and provide important survival benefits. Therefore, understanding the UPR is relevant to study of pathophysiology. In metazoans the UPR comprises three limbs, each activated by a separate class of ER membrane protein. IREI and ATF6 each initiate a separate gene expression cascade in response to ER stress. These lead to adaptive responses including increased levels of chaperone synthesis, which are well understood. The third protein that signals ER stress, PERK, is a protein kinase that phosphorylates the eukaryotic initiation factor 2 complex (eIF2), inhibiting translation initiation. This has two consequences. (1) ER client protein synthesis is reduced, relieving some of the load off the organelle. (2) limiting eIF2 activity favours the translation of specific mRNAs including those encoding the transcription factor ATF4, leading to a gene expression cascade that is controlled by eIF2 phosphorylation. It has been shown that eIF2 phosphorylation is a common pathway in a number of stress responses, including ER stress, viral infection, nutritional deprivation and oxidative stress. It has consequently been termed as Integrated Stress Response (ISR). Three observations by the host lab serve as the point of departure for our proposed study. PERK-/- cells are exquisitely sensitive to oxidative stress, to such an extent that they are only viable when reducing agents are added to the medium. Finally, preliminary screens have implicated heme-oxygenase 1 (HO-1) as a potential candidate downstream effector of the ISR. This enzyme has previously been shown to be involved in the response to oxidative stress, but has not previously been known to be part of the UPR. My goal is to understand the molecular basis for the survival benefits provided by the integrated stress response to cells experiencing ER stress. I hypothesize that the downstream target genes of the integrated stress response are essential to this survival benefit. This hypothesis will be tested in the following ways. I shall test the ability of HO-1 to rescue the phenotype of cells defective in the proximal components of the ISR, ie. PERK-/- and ATF4-/- cells, by transfection with HO-1 expression pasmids. Parameters to be measured will include cell survival during ER stress, reactive oxygen species accumulation and the ability of ATF4-/- cells to withstand the removal of reducing agents from the medium. The resistance of HO-1-/- cells to ER stress will be studied through exposure to agents such as tunicamycin that impair protein folding. I predict that it will be impaired. Identification of further genes capable of suppressing the hypersensitivity of ISR defective cells to ER stress will be performed through somatic gene screening methods well established in the host lab. I shall also endeavour to identify target genes of the ISR triggered by ER stress in wildtype but not ISR defective cells through microarray analysis.

title: Life course influences on women's urinary symptoms and their management during the menopause transition: a prospective birth cohort study.
description: The MRC National Survey of Health and Development (NSHD) is a nationally representative sample of 2547 women and 2815 men followed up regularly since their birth in March 1946. We shall use repeated data on urinary incontinence collected annually from women study members between the ages of 48 and 54 years, together with life course data on development, health and circumstances, to study the effects of childhood enuresis phenotypes, lifetime weight trajectories and timing of menopausal transition on urge and stress incontinence. Previous, mainly cross sectional studies, focused on adult risk factors, and could not distinguish the effects of menopause from those of age. We shall examine whether changes in urinary symptoms impact on quality of life, independent of potential confounders. We shall study the management strategies that women adopt to relieve urinary symptoms, identifying long-term socioeconomic, behavioural, and health characteristics that distinguish between various management strategies, and between those who seek help or not. This life course study will advance aetiological understanding of midlife incontinence and help clinicians tailor treatment strategies to an individual woman's risk profile. It will inform policy for well-timed interventions designed to improve quality of life for women as they negotiate the menopausal years.

title: Dopaminergic and cholinergic neuromodulation of novelty encoding in humans.
description: The ability to memorize preferentially novel stimuli is essential for survivalin a changing environment. The cognitive and neuromodulatory brain mechanisms behind this preference are still unclear. On the basis of our recent work, we take the view that motivation, reinforcement and prediction- errors are key factors in the preferential encoding of novelty. We hypothesize that when a novel stimulus is detected, brain networks specializing in processing motivationally relevant and potentially rewarding stimuli are activated, that includes dopaminergic and cholinergic circuitry. The resulting dopaminergic and cholinergic activation modulates long term plasticity in memory-relevant structures such as the medial temporal lobes. On the basis of these hypotheses, we now aim to identify the mechanisms and cognitive processes through which dopaminergic and cholinergic modulation improve long- term memoryformation for novel stimuli. To that end we will use multimodal pharmacological imaging (functional magnetic resonance imaging and magnetoencephalography) involving dopaminergic and cholinergic drugs in experiments that allow us to contrast the influence of novelty with reinforcement-value and prediction-error, and assess how they interact in memory formation in healthy adults. The results may help in understanding and treating memory impairment associated with neuromodulatory dysfunction in aging and neurodegenerative neurological conditions.

title: Request to support a conference titled 'Infectious diseases of the nervous system: pathogenesis and worldwide impact' to be held on 2-4 May 2008.
description: Conference " Infectious diseases of the nervous system: pathogenesis and worldwide impact" to be held September 10 to 13 at the Pasteur Institute in Paris. In comparison to studies on infectious diseases of the nervous system in western societies, studies on such diseases in the developing world have been relatively neglected. This is paradoxical as neurotropic pathogens are frequent in the developing world and contribute significantly to human suffering and disease burden. More over living with neurological handicap and /or cognitive dysfunction is likely to have an impact on socio-economic development. Since the NINDS mission is to reduce the burden of neurological diseases for people world wide, the pathogenesis, diagnosis and treatment of neurological infectious diseases should be a high priority for the institute. To our knowledge this topic has not been covered by a meeting in a broad, comprehensive way.Therefore we propose to hold a Conference on " Infectious Diseases of the nervous system: pathogenesis and world impact". Such a conference should enhance knowledge in the field and promote exchanges between medical research centers in developing and tropical regions with western Institutes actively working in the field. Our objectives are to create a multidisciplinary dialogue between (1) clinicians studying nervous system infections and their impact on neural and cognitive functions in renowned Medical Centers and Institutes in the western and developing world; (2) scientists working on the life cycle and molecular make-up of neurotropic infectious agents and their vectors; (3) neuroscientists investigating these pathogen interactions with the blood brain barrier and neural cells; (4) immunologists studying the innate and adaptive immune response to neurotropic pathogens: (5) experts in new technologies for diagnosis and therapies; (6) medical anthropologists. One major point to consider throughout this conference is that the central nervous system is usually not the primary target site of the pathogen. Therefore a window of opportunity exists to interfere with pathogen spreading. In contrast, the peripheral nervous system can be a direct site of entry from the skin in the case of rabies and leprosy where the pathogen invades peripheral nerves. Rabies virus then moves rapidly along nerves to the central nervous system.

title: CEREBRAL MECHANISMS UNDERLYING COGNITIVE DYSFUNCTION IN AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS.
description: This study aims to define the structural basis of cognitive abnormalities in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), by clarifying the relative involvement of specific cognitive domains and the respective contribution of selective white matter tract and cortical damage to cognitive impairment, using a combination of diffusion tensor magnetic resonance imaging (DT-MRI) and volumetric analysis. We will apply DT-MRI to study white matter changes underlying cognitive dysfunction in ALS. Given our previ ous imaging findings we will, by comparing 30 ALS patients with 30 normal controls, test the hypothesis that specific disconnection mechanisms underlie cognitive deficits in ALS. We predict that ALS patients will demonstrate vulnerability primarily in frontal association fibres. Tract-specific measures of fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity will be compared between groups. By concurrently undertaking detailed neuropsychological assessment of executive function, language and memory, the us e of multivariate analysis will also permit the exploration of correlations between the integrity of intralobar frontal, frontal-striatal, fronto-limbic and perisylvian language pathways and their relationship to these cognitive domains. This study will further understanding of the pathophysiology of cognitive impairment in ALS, and provide new insights into phenotypic variation in ALS by identifying markers of white as well as grey matter vulnerability.

title: Conference: Autism 2020.
description: Prior's Court Foundation is at the forefront of autism provision for five to nineteen year olds. With this event we aim to consolidate developments in autism in both the education and research sectors and stimulate discussion on the future directions for all working with autism. There have been a number of recent conferences specific to autism research, but this conference will give an engaging view of what has led to the current state of the autism knowledge and will be wholly accessible to parents, professionals and practitioners alike. By bringing advancements made since the earliest descriptions of autism together with present trends in research and practice the conference will allow reflection on the direction of Autism in the future, hence the title' Autism 2020'. The conference will be the inaugural vent in the Dame Stephanie Shirley Lecture Series and as founding patron and an influential figure in the autism field, Dame Stephanie will give the opening address.

title: The Kiss of Light: Nursing and Light Therapy in 20th-Century Britain.
description: 'The Kiss of Light' is an exciting collaboration between a well-established small museum and the Centre for the History of Medicine at Warwick University, principally Dr Tania Woloshyn, a Wellcome Trust-funded Research Fellow and specialist in the history of light therapy. Through a shared commitment to engaging the public by examining historic medical treatments and questioning their contemporary relevance, we aim to show how perceptions of light have changed over time and been shaped by both e nthusiasm and fear. Over the 12 weeks of the exhibition, we will display a diverse range of British images, objects and texts about sunlight therapy (heliotherapy) and artificial light therapy (phototherapy) in a visually inspiring way. Highlighting the role of nurses as key agents and children as vulnerable patients in light therapy's history, our project aims to excavate a forgotten past and to provoke discussion about medical agency and patient care. Through its interpretation and engagem ent programme aimed at the museum's key audiences, the exhibition aspires to prompt visitors to think critically about light's healing powers and risks, about ongoing debates on light for wellbeing, as beautifying, curative or dangerous, and to question the voices disseminating these beliefs. The museum's location in St Thomas Hospital enables us to work with healthcare professionals who use light as a treatment for mental and physical health today. By using the very subject of the exhibitio n, namely light, to display the historic material, we will illuminate this subject both intellectually and aesthetically.

title: Early bedside biomarkers of cognitive function following neonatal brain injury.
description: Perinatal brain injury remains a significant cause of neonatal mortality and is associated with long-term neurological disabilities including cognitive impairment, mental retardation and accounts for 15 to 28% of children with cerebral palsy. There is an urgent clinical need to detect as early as possible those neonates at most risk and who may benefit from adjunct therapies and/or redirection of clinical care for effective rehabilitation. Early detection and assessment of brain neurological sta tus and outcome requires sensitive, robust and easy to measure biomarkers. The aims of my fellowship are to: (1) develop new methods for assessing neonatal brain injury and deliver early bedside biomarkers of atypical cognitive and neurological development; (2) inform and access efficacy of targeted interventions and clinical management for long-term neurological outcome in brain injured neonates through a clinical evaluation program. For several years now I have been developing instrumentati on and methodology that can non-invasively measure brain tissue oxygenation, haemodynamics and uniquely assess mitochondrial oxygenation through measurement of the oxidation status of cytochrome-c-oxidase (oxCCO). We have shown recently that, utilising our novel multimodal measurements that combine optics and magnetic resonance spectroscopy, in the neonatal animal model, the oxCCO measurement is a good indicator of the biochemical status of the brain and is directly related to recovery and outco me following brain hypoxic-ischaemia. This Fellowship will enable me to build upon my previous achievements and embark on an ambitious program of research to clinical evaluate and establish the brain optical measurement of oxCCO as a neuromonitoring biomarker.

title: Wellcome Trust Engagement Fellowship 2014.
description: Practice-Led Elements Being a creator is about making and doing, reading, questioning, dialogue and rehearsing. Embedding practice in the Fellowship model is, therefore, fundamental: Inspirational: A Tragedy The National Theatre Studio has awarded me an Attachment in Oct/Nov 2014, on a large-scale new work with directed cast. The premise is an examination of ways in which circumstance, illness or disability are utilised to ?inspire' others. With a humorous, intimate look at ?inspiration porn', national fundraising campaigns, the symbols and signifiers of illness and our expectations of role models, this work will provoke public conversation around pity and charity marketing. The Fellowship enables development time; however, the realisation is budget- free due to NT support. A further development is planned in Spring 2015 with the premiere in 2016. Fun with Cancer Patients This is a research methodology to enable access the psychosocial experience, a vehicle for patient voices and a way to seed small communities of facilitators, leaders and thinkers UK wide. A reformulation of an existing successful project, 2-day workshops roll out to six different cities. Performance workshops take place with different focal groups experiencing cancer, e.g. LGBT patients, parents, ethnic minority groups and people with disabilities. This builds to a touring exhibition from September 2015 to May 2016, accompanied by further workshops, co-facilitated with local participants, talks and other events, creating extensive, high quality engagement and building stronger networks based on multiple interactions. Knowledge Building and Profile Development The Fellowship gives time and context to observe a number of clinical education classes. While I work regularly with medical professionals, I am the ?other', a rare moment when trainees talk about patient experience, though the profession itself strongly influences attitudes towards care. Moments to learn more are the OSCE exam preparation-how we take histories, talk about diagnoses, break news; and biology classes surrounding the diagnosis and treatment of cancer. I propose to observe an OSCE prep class and mock exam, facilitated via Performing Medicine and oncology classes at Barts & The London School, facilitated via Dr David Prowse. For both, I aim to reciprocate with talks on my own work. GP, comedian and journalist Dr Phil Hammond (Trust Me, I'm a Doctor) has kindly offered to mentor me. We will meet quarterly. A Strategic Steering Group will be convened in order to better understand and access the national networks surrounding illness, cancer, the NHS and the Arts. Confirmed members include Shonagh Manson (Jerwood Charitable Foundation), Zoe Alton (Teenage Cancer Trust), Amynta Cardwell (Consultant on Organisational Learning for Central and Northwest London NHS), and representation from education and medical humanities. I will also continue my relationship as an Associate Artist with Performing Medicine. From The Wellcome Trust, exploring the Wellcome Collection for historic attitudes to cancer will be highly informative, as will accessing the Fellows network for a broader knowledge base across illnesses outside cancer. Inspired by works such as Sick City, I am also excited to be developing ideas for an innovative publication aimed at a public audience.

title: Longitudinal evidence on the longer-term impacts of environmental change on population health and nutrition
description: Little is known about long-term effects of environmental disasters on population health. We will measure impacts, after 10 years, of the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami on biological health risks leveraging data from the Study of the Tsunami Aftermath and Recovery (STAR), an on-going large- scale longitudinal population-representative survey of individuals who lived (when the tsunami struck) along the coast of Sumatra, Indonesia. Baseline interviews 10 months pretsunami are combined with 5 annual follow-ups and a 10-year follow-up. We have interviewed over 96% of the 30,000 surviving baseline respondents. To provide rigorous evidence on the disaster’s longer- term impacts, this pilot study collects key biological health and nutrition markers implicated in major non-communicable diseases, and links them to the roles of stresses from tsunami exposure and compromised psycho-social health. Moreover, we investigate behavioural adaption in response to the environmental destruction of the tsunami and reconstruction after the tsunami. Looking forward, this research program provides an ideal platform to develop an international inter-disciplinary model laboratory, leveraging STAR with other resources, to investigate the consequences of environmental and climate- related changes and also conduct interventions to provide the evidence-base necessary to design innovations likely to have a sustained impact on population health and well-being.

title: Factors influencing cognition and ageing in a simple model organism
description: We plan to study longevity and cognition in a simple model organism, the nematode C. elegans. Nematodes will be raised on different bacterial food substrates, which the co-supervisor's lab have shown affects the life-span of the worm. We will test associative learning across the lifespan in these differently-fed worms to establish whether cognitive function is preserved even in the long-lived nematodes. In parallel, we will test various compounds that have cognition-enhancing properties in mammals to see if they rescue cognitive decline associated with ageing in the nematode. Key goals will be: The establishment of an associative learning protocol in the worm Demonstration of changes in longevity associated with mutations of genes in C. elegans Demonstration that different food substrates affect longevity Demonstration that nootropics influence cognition across the lifespan

title: University of Edinburgh - Translational Neuroscience
description: The main aim of this project is to characterise the effects of FMR1 repeat expansion mutations on astrocytes using human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) models. FMR1 codes for FMRP, which controls activity-dependent neurodevelopment through affecting cellular processes such as transcription, translation and ion channel dynamics (1). In Fragile X Syndrome (FXS) there is reduced FMRP expression due to translational repression of FMR1 (2).While most research on FXS has focused on cell-autonomous effects of FMR1 mutations in neurones (2), FMR1 is also expressed in glial cells, with particularly high transcript levels present in astrocytes (3). Furthermore, astrocyte-specific and global knockout (KO) mice show similar neuronal and behavioural abnormalities (4); as selective expression of Fmr1 in astrocytes alone fails to rescue the disease phenotype (4), normal brain function therefore appears to require FMR1 expression in both cell types. This notion is also supported by mouse co-culture experiments, where Fmr1 KO astrocytes and neurones induce defects in wild-type (WT) neurones and astrocytes, respectively, while some of the pathology seen in the KO cells is simultaneously alleviated (5-7).This study therefore aims to answer the following questions: - Can the deficits seen in Fmr1 KO mouse models be replicated in hiPSC-derived astrocytes harbouring the FMR1 repeat expansion mutation? \- What are the key pathways affected in human FXS astrocytes leading to the cellular phenotypes observed? \- To what extent are the deficits seen in neurons and astrocytes in the FXS brain due to non-cell autonomous effects that they may exert on each other? This project emerges from previous work we have done on FXS and non-cell autonomous mechanisms of neurological disease. We have characterised cellular, transcriptomic and translatomic changes in FXS rodent models (8-10), and have recently established three FXS patient hiPSC lines, and one FMR1 KO embryonic stem cell (ESC) line. Furthermore, we have published protocols for generating astrocytes and cortical neurones from hiPSCs (11-12), and have studied non- cell autonomous mechanisms of other repeat-expansion diseases using such models (12). Lastly, we have recently created a multi-species co-culture technique for analysis of non-cell autonomous effects on the transcriptome of neurones and astrocytes (13).We will begin approaching the research questions by generating isogenic controls for the three pre-existing FXS patient hiPSC lines using CRISPR/Cas9 technology. Using all three isogenic pairs will allow us to identify pathological changes that are shared between patients, and which result from a loss of FMR1 expression. These cell lines will be used to generate cortical astrocytes with and without the repeat expansion mutation, comparisons between which will be made to dissect cell-autonomous effects of FMR1 mutations on astrocytes. This will include study of the overt cellular phenotype through assays for cell viability, structure, function and metabolism. These experiments may then be confirmed in the FMR1 KO ESC line.The molecular mechanisms which may underlie these phenotypic changes will then be dissected with transcriptome analysis of the iPSC lines. Differentially expressed genes will be identified with RNAseq, and subjected to gene ontology analysis in order to identify main cellular pathways that are altered in FXS astrocytes. This will provide guidance for further study of the cellular defects seen in FXS.Cortical neurones will also be generated from the iPSC lines, and co-culture models of WT neurones and mutant astrocytes, and vice versa, will be employed for the study of non-cell autonomous mechanisms of FXS. As before, comparisons will be made between cell viability, structure, function and metabolism. Furthermore, co-cultures of hiPSC and primary cultures of rat neurones and astrocytes will be used for the study of cell- type specific changes to transcriptomes in such systems (13).As we are currently developing cerebral organoid models of FXS, these interactions could potentially be explored further in this model. We are also currently refining protocols for generating FXS microglia and oligodendrocytes, in which FXS effects could also be studied. The planned timeframe for these experiments is as follows:Year 1: Generation of control lines through correction of FMR1 mutation in patient iPSCs Differentiation and characterisation of cortical neurons and astrocytesYears 1-2: Study of cell-autonomous effects of FMR1 mutations on astrocytesYears 2-3: Study of non-cell autonomous effects of FMR1 mutations on neurones and astrocytes

title: The cognitive neuroscience of over-eating: normative and clinical studies of goal-driven and stimulus-driven responses
description: There is a pressing need to understand the phenotypic variations of obesity in order to elucidate the diverse pathways and mechanisms by which it arises and, ultimately, to offer suitably tailored interventions. My proposed work aims to provide insights into the cognitive neuroscience of health-harming over- consumption. Its ultimate goals are to characterise cognitive mechanisms underlying eating behaviours, exploring how these are selected and deployed in ways that are shaped by both internal and environmental signals. The work is based on the view that obesity is ultimately driven by a complex integration of environmental and bodily signals and that a comprehensive approach must characterise this integration in order to determine how it may be altered in over-eating. My proposal has the following goals: \- To understand how stimulus-driven (automatic) and goal-directed (reflective) reward behaviours are balanced in relation to eating choices and to explore how this balance may differ across hungry and sated, lean and obese people. \- To relate these underlying processes to hormonal/metabolic signals as well and to real-world eating choices. \- To characterise the effects of three specific perturbations to this integrated system: (i) elective gastrectomy, (ii) single gene mutations affecting hypothalamic circuitry and (iii) psychopharmacological manipulations

title: Measuring stress in the endoplasmic reticulum caused by rhodopsin retinitis pigmentosa mutants
description: Most rhodopsin autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa (ADRP) mutants are thought to misfold in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) of rod photoreceptor cells. Protein folding quality control machinery (QCM) in the ER supports proper folding of defective rhodopsin or targets them for removal via the endoplasmic reticulum-associated protein degradation (ERAD) system. However, when the QCM is overwhelmed by large quanties of defective rhodopsin receptors, apoptosis, rod cell death and retinitis pigmentosa occurs. Cells monitor misfolded protein content in the ER using the unfolded protein response (UPR). Three mechanisms of UPR exist in mammalian cells: ATF6, IRE-1 and PERK, all of which are activated in response to ER stress. IRE-1 is a resident ER transmembrane protein that when activated splices out an intron from the XBP1 mRNA transcript. This cytoplasmic splicing event leads to production of an in-frame transcript, enabling translation of full length XBP-1 transcription factor that controls gene expression to regulate ER stress. We will use hybrid genes containing the XBP-1 gene (containing the intron) fused to the N-terminus of nano-Luc and GFP genes. Expression of ADRP rhodopsin mutants in cells containing these XBP-1-miniLuc or -GFP reporters allows us to visualise and quantify the degree of ER stress induced.

title: Epidemiology of Tungiasis in Kenya
description: Tungiasis is an extremely Neglected Tropical Disease and has received little attention from researchers, granting bodies, and government Departments of Health. It is caused by the sand flea, Tunga penetrans, the female of which burrows into the epidermis, mostly of the feet, where it grows 2000 fold in 7 days, inducing severe inflammation, immense pain and itching. Chronic re- infection leads to severe morbidity. Although it is known to occur mostly in children under 15 years in marginalized, resource poor communities in the Caribbean, South America and Sub-Saharan Africa, not a single country knows its national prevalence, nor impact on its population. I am proposing to conduct the first ever national prevalence survey in Kenya using a cross- sectional, randomized, stratified cluster design of 10,950 students in primary schools. The survey will be repeated in the dry and wet seasons to investigate the seasonality of transmission. A sub-sample of infected and uninfected students will be selected to determine the impact tungiasis has on the quality of life, cognitive development and educational achievement. Interviews with teachers and students will investigate possible risk factors for severe disease. The goal is to provide information to mobilize resources and guide policy development for control programs.

title: Understanding the role of PARPs in replication-associated DNA damage repair.
description: DNA is constantly exposed to endogenous and exogenous damaging agents. It is necessary to repair such damage to prevent the accumulation of mutations. The poly ADP-ribose polymerase (PARP) family of proteins mediate such repair processes by post-translationally modifying target proteins with ADP-ribose moieties. PARP activity, specifically PARP1, is most widely associated with single strand break repair, however, it is increasingly apparent other PARPs act within multiple repair pathways. Building on work done in this group establishing a role for PARPs in the resolution of replication-associated damage, I aim to understand the mechanisms by which PARPs interact with their substrates to promote error-free DNA replication. I will use immunoprecipitation and affinity purification strategies to assess the ADP- ribosylation status of candidate proteins in cells experiencing replication stress. Coupling these approaches to mass spectrometry analysis will allow me to identify PARP substrates in a global, unbiased fashion and specifically map modified residues. To gain mechanistic insight into this PARP-mediated regulation, I will mutate ADP-ribosylation sites using genome editing and assess the efficiency and dynamics of replication repair. Aberrant repair of DNA damage increases genomic instability and heightens tumorigenesis risk therefore my findings will provide vital information for the development of novel cancer therapeutics.

title: Understanding the link between oxidative stress, microtubule aberrations and neuronal ageing.
description: With the ever-ageing population, research efforts are being driven towards understanding the mechanisms which mediate the ageing process with a particular focus in the context of neurons due to the association and debilitating manifestation of many neurodegenerative disorders. The accumulation of damage to tissues over time due to excess reactive oxygen species is a prominent theory of ageing and will be the focus of this project. We will utilise the common fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster) to elucidate critical conserved genetic pathways impacted by the overproduction of oxidative compounds and to understand how this affects the neuronal microtubule cytoskeleton which is important for neuronal structure and function, and axonal transport of essential molecules and organelles. Research using Drosophila provides a deep insight into the inner functioning of neurons within the brain and share remarkable similarities in neurophysiology and brain organisation to mammalians. The fly genetic composition will be manipulated to remove or edit the function of several age-related genes to understand their role in stress-mediated damage to neurons and the underlying mechanisms. From this, we may identify novel protein targets capable of genetic or pharmaceutical manipulation to serve neuroprotective benefits, providing possible method of treatment.

title: The overlapping genetic architecture of platelet granularity and neurodevelopmental disorders
description: Platelets are blood cells needed for clot formation. Neurons are brain cells which transmit information through chemical signals. Although they have different roles in the body, platelets and neurons both function by releasing tiny substance-filled packages called granules. Previous research has shown that similar genes control this process in both cell types. Autism is a neuron disorder which affects the way individuals interact with the world. The genes causing autism are poorly understood but are thought to be involved in the formation of neuron granules. Platelet genes are better understood. I plan to use the similarities between platelet and neuron granules to identify new genes causing autism. In the longer term, we hope this research leads to improvements in diagnosing and treating the disorder. My research builds on data showing that differences between healthy people in the number of granules in platelets are linked to subtle changes in genes. I will analyse lists of these genetic changes and select those most likely to be involved in both platelet granule formation and autism. For the most promising genetic change, I will alter this gene in cells in the laboratory to see if this affects granules, and therefore could contribute to autism.

title: Molecular Mechanisms in PCDH19 Regulation of Cortical Neurogenesis
description: Genetic changes (mutations) in the gene Protocadherin-19 (PCDH19) - located on the X-chromosome - are associated with Epileptic Encephalopathy Early Infantile 9 (EIEE9), a rare genetic disease that causes early onset epilepsy and cognitive impairment in heterozygous females (females that carry a normal and a mutant copy of PCDH19). To date, little is known about how this phenomenon causes EIEE9, however the early onset of the disorder suggests a neurodevelopmental basis. Using genetically-altered mice, we have shown that Pcdh19 has a critical role in brain development by helping primordial brain cells called progenitors communicate with each other and transition into mature nerve cells, an event called neurogenesis. We also found that progenitors that express Pcdh19 and progenitors that do not express Pcdh19 produce significantly less and more nerve cells, respectively, but only in the developing brains of heterozygous female mice, which may be the underlying factor of EIEE9. To explore this further, we aim to discover the significant molecular pathways that Pcdh19 might be involved in to regulate neurogenesis using candidate and unbiased approaches. The results from this project will provide new insight into the roles of Pcdh19 during brain development and highlight potential targets for EIEE9 therapeutic intervention.

title: British Academy Small Research Grant, Conference and Policy Workshop Proposal
description: The British Academy is submitting a funding proposal to the Wellcome Trust which will provide support for researchers in the humanities and social sciences working in areas related to health and wellbeing. Taking a broad definition of health, the proposal will provide a portfolio of support for academics, at all stages of their careers, working in the humanities and social sciences by providing funding for Small Research Grants, academic conferences and policy workshops. The proposal follows discussions with the Trust over a number of months and is valued at £3.97 million including: funding of £2.76 million for Small Research grants; £1.12 million for conferences; and £84,000 for policy workshops (over 3 years). Funding is proposed to begin in early 2020 and to finish in 2026. The collaboration is designed to demonstrate the relevance of humanities and social science research in relation to health and wellbeing through the scale and breadth of funding options for researchers and the potential for long term impact.

title: Factors of biological ageing: does it all go together when it goes?
description: Ageing-related cognitive decline carries a huge personal, societal, and financial cost. Understanding its underlying mechanisms with a view to ameliorating age-related cognitive decline is a huge challenge. It is essential to identify biomarkers of cognitive ageing and their potential determinants. Brain structural imaging markers in older age, their correspondence with proteomic and other biomarkers, and their potential determinants, are poorly characterised. Our understanding is informed by cross-sectional studies (which cannot fully reflect the dynamic within-person processes of ageing) and mainly univariate longitudinal data (i.e. describing how brain regions individually decline over time): most aspects of brain structure decline, on average. However, these approaches do not tell us whether there are important patterns of coordinated change, nor are they well- aligned with other levels of biological explanation. Such information could potentially aid stratification of risk and identification of important clusters of determinants of brain and cognitive ageing. I will apply cutting- edge factor-analytic methods to large longitudinal datasets to detect and validate patterns of correlated biological changes (brain structure, serum proteomic and DNA transcriptomic). I will test how these dimensions of ageing are associated with each other and with cognitive ageing, and use several techniques to ascertain their lifestyle, genetic and epigenetic predictors.

title: The transcriptomic landscape of the human heart
description: Although we think of it as a muscle, the heart is comprised of highly distinct subunits, as diverse as valves and pacemaker tissue. All these tissues are made from only 11 types of cell. The effects of disease and ageing on the heart can be partly understood by assessing changes in these cell populations and the signature sets of genes they express, however it is vital to first characterise the healthy organ as a reference for what goes awry under different conditions. Single-cell technologies allow us to dissociate tissues into their constituent cells and determine their type, expression profile (transcriptome), and protein levels (proteome). The Teichmann group have already produced a preliminary atlas of the cell types in the adult human heart. This initial data shows the variations in cell types between anatomic sites within the heart. However, this healthy heart atlas covers a limited subset of the tissues in the heart. I will (a) expand the scope of the healthy heart atlas and (b) compare this with tissue from hearts affected by disease or put under stress. This will show the changes in cell populations and their function under these conditions – highlighting potential targets for therapies.

title: Physiological and behavioral functions of the basal ganglia
description: The basal ganglia are implicated in a wide range of behaviors and are particularly important for many types of learning. The diversity of basal ganglia function is tied to cortical diversity; indeed, the entire cortex outputs to the basal ganglia, which is routed in a loop via the thalamus back to the cortex. These three components of the cortex, basal ganglia, and thalamus likely form an archetypal circuit which carries out similar computations in the perceptual, cognitive, and motor domains. The way in which activity propagates across these structures, and how this propagation changes to support learning, are largely unknown. I propose to investigate the interdependence within this circuit by building on my prior work on communication between the cortex and striatum. In those experiments, I developed methodology towards defining the functional relationship between structures, and identified specific learning-induced changes. Here, I will trace those changes across structures throughout learning, I will determine how these changes affect the little-studied output arm of the basal ganglia, and I will causally determine which connections within this circuit drive specific components of both activity and learned behavior. These experiments will contribute toward a holistic understanding of a major neural circuit.

title: Hippocampal navigation and place recognition
description: The existence of place, directional, boundary and grid cells in the rat hippocampal formation provides strong evidence that it functions as a cognitive map containing map-like representations of familiar environments which enable the animal to identify its current location together with desirable and undesirable locations, and to move towards or away from these. Using our newly developed honeycomb maze, we have shown that the CA1 place cells support flexible navigation by pointing the direction to the goal and, in addition, evaluating the suitability of all non-goalward directions as possible options if the goalward choice is not available. We plan to explore the properties of this representation, its environmental and path integation inputs and the way in which it underpins flexible navigation. We have also shown that the CA1 place cells are sensitive to the size of the environment. Their firing rates are modulated by a range of environmental sizes with some cells preferring small environments, others intermediate sized ones, and yet others firing only to the largest environment. We will study exactly which aspect of environmental size and shape these cells are monitoring and how they are doing so.

title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Incarceration’s racialized health impacts in Latin America
description: Incarceration has vast and unequal impact on Black and white health and wellbeing. Research conducted primarily in North America describes incarceration’s racialized impacts beyond prison walls, where racial minority families are locked into racialized and durable cycles of disadvantage. Yet in Latin America, the links between incarceration, racism, and human health and wellbeing are both underexamined and misunderstood. The region is frequently mischaracterized as homogenously ‘mixed race’ rather than racially plural, and existing research focuses on disease outbreaks inside prisons, omitting incarceration’s family- and community-level health impacts. This mixed-methods program of community-based participatory research will illuminate incarceration’s racialized health impacts in Latin America. Working with a cross-national multi-sectoral network of stakeholders, it uses newly available racial disparities data to create the first ever portrait of racial inequality across prisons and community health in Colombia, Mexico, and Puerto Rico. Comparative ethnography in Colombia, Mexico, and Puerto Rico maps and conceptualizes how incarceration perpetuates racially unequal profiles of health and wellbeing among families and communities. Community partners participate in the development of public engagement strategies to shape public conversation about incarceration’s impacts at the local level, culminating in policy recommendations for mitigating the community-level harms associated with racialized systems of incarceration.

title: ‘Just who do I leave my worldly possessions to, darling?’: A Study of Queer Inheritance
description: Inheritance - the right to bequeath one’s estate to whomever one chooses is at the heart of end-of-life wellbeing and a cornerstone of a ‘good death’. This project examines what inheritance looks like and means for queer people and communities, and asks why inheritance, and indeed disinheritance, are such meaning making sites - beset with traumas, fears and anxieties – and at the same time, foundational to Queer survivance, joy and wellbeing. The key goal of the project is to establish QUEER.UK; a radical space for transformation and societal impact rooted in scholarly explorations of queer health, death and wellbeing that is at its core, intersectional, cross generational, focused on multiplicities of ethnicities, genders, religions and classes. The research network QUEER.UK will focus initially on the question and practices of queer inheritances: what and how queer people pass onto others and how this can contribute towards a sense of queer wellbeing that bridges life and death. QUEER.UK will allow me to create a meaningful scholarly environment through the time, resources and networking opportunities allowed by the Grant and build a portfolio of publications and KEI events, apply for further funding and to build the case for career promotion.

title: ARTFUL AGEING: Investigating ageing mechanisms in children growing up with HIV in the era of antiretroviral therapy
description: We will determine how the mechanisms underlying biological ageing limit trajectories of growth, physical and cognitive function in children growing up with HIV. Despite antiretroviral therapy (ART) successes, children with HIV (CWH) commonly experience multi-system comorbidities limiting growth, physical and cognitive function, with phenotypes reminiscent of those seen in older adults. In older adults, Geroscience has identified a discrete set of hallmarks of biological ageing (primary, antagonistic and integrative) responsible for a common systemic susceptibility to disease. We hypothesize that perinatally-acquired HIV infection causes Accelerated Biological Ageing in children which drives poorer long-term health and development. Within a 24-month prospective cohort study recruiting 800 children aged 6-9 years in Harare (400 CWH on ART, and 400 HIV-negative and unexposed), our objectives are to: 1\. Quantify domain-specific deficits (growth, physical, cognitive) in CWH, compared to their uninfected peers, longitudinally. 2\. Characterise hallmarks of biological ageing in children with and without HIV. 3\. Determine the role of accelerated hallmarks of biological ageing in explaining domain- specific deficits longitudinally in CWH. 4\. Identify gero-protectors and gero-drivers potentially amenable to future therapeutic interventions. Our innovative South-North consortium melds HIV physicians, paediatricians, geriatricians and experts in geroscience to ‘Discover the Science’ behind paediatric HIV-associated ageing.
recipient: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

title: Intestinal Inflammation in Malaria and Malaria-Schistosomiasis Co-Infection.
description: Diarrhoea is a less-recognised feature of malaria, yet the underlying mechanism remains unknown. To investigate this, the cellular and immunological pathology of intestinal inflammation in malaria will be characterised using two murine models: P.chabaudi AS (‘uncomplicated’) and P.chabaudi CB (‘severe’). Changes in cellular populations and gene expression in the small intestine will be determined by flow cytometry and single-cell genomics. As co-infection with malaria and Schistosomiasis mansoni is found in >90% of Ugandan children, the impact of co-infection will be explored in a novel P.chabaudi/S.mansoni murine co-infection model. Serum cytokines and faecal biomarkers of inflammation will be assessed using Olink cytokine multiplexing, traditional ELISA and flow cytometry. While animal work is ongoing, a cross- sectional field study of Ugandan schoolchildren will be undertaken from an area with endemic malaria and schistosomiasis. For the first time, faecal biomarkers of inflammation will be assessed in acutely infected children to determine the clinical features associated with human malaria-induced diarrhoea and its impact on S.mansoni co-infection. Overall, this project seeks to understand the mechanistic basis of the gastrointestinal immunopathology of malaria and malaria-schistosomiasis coinfection which could lead to the development of new therapeutic strategies to restore intestinal health promoting childhood well-being.

title: Plant-based nutritional strategies for optimising human performance in the heat.
description: Carbohydrate (CHO) availability is critical for sustaining physical performance, especially in hot environments where thermoregulatory and metabolic demands are elevated. High-glycaemic index (GI) CHOs such as glucose or maltodextrin provide rapid energy, but may trigger reactive hypoglycaemia, gastrointestinal discomfort, and increased cardiovascular strain due to a greater reliance on anaerobic metabolism. These effects can impair endurance, compromise gut integrity, and elevate systemic stress. In contrast, low-GI CHOs promote slower, more stable glucose release, potentially supporting sustained energy delivery and reducing fatigue, metabolic disruption, and thermal strain. While the effects of CHO availability on performance are well established, there is limited understanding of how CHO GI specifically influences thermoregulatory responses (e.g., core temperature, sweat rate), cardiovascular load, gastrointestinal tolerance, and perceived effort during exercise in the heat. These relationships remain poorly defined, despite their relevance for performance and health, in the context of climate change. This project will examine how high- vs low-GI carbohydrates affect physiological, metabolic, and thermoregulatory responses during treadmill walking in the heat. Findings will inform nutritional strategies to support physical work capacity, thermal resilience, and recovery for individuals operating in heat- stressed environments, with practical implications for military, occupational, and athletic populations amid rising global temperatures.

title: Functional genomics for Trypanosoma brucei.
description: 1\. Trypanosoma brucei, a protozoan parasite and the causative agent of African sleeping sickness and Nagana, is a major human and animal pathogen. It is an important model system for parasite biology, closely related to Leishmania and T. cruzi, and is extremely well supported by a network of ~20 UK-based laboratories. This application seeks to build upon the genome sequencing efforts and to establish a collection of parasites for postgenomic functional study. There are three aims of the present application: To utilise the information from the Trypanosoma brucei genome projects to produce a research resource and systematic collection of mutants by targeted gene inactivation using RNAi. To undertake a functional characterisation of the mutant collection in a systematic manner, making strains and data fully and rapidly available to the research community. To develop and establish methods and standard operating procedures for a genome wide analysis of gene function in T. brucei.

title: The biological role of the Cdk5 and Pak1 kinases in the developing cortex.
description: The development of the mammalian cerebral cortex depends on a number of signalling pathways, the complexities of which are only beginning to emerge. We study the Cdk5 and Pak1 kinases that are known regulators of the neuronal cytoskeleton. In the cortex the Cdk5 kinase is essential for neuronal migration, axon and dendrite morphology, while the role of Pak1 is currently less understood. We have shown that the Cdk5 kinase phosphorylates Pak1 on a unique site, which is important for the regulation of neurite morphology. The mitotic cyclin B/Cdc2 kinase also catalyses this phosphorylation in neuronal progenitors. Our aim is to investigate: 1) The signalling pathways that regulate Cdk5 and Pak1 We will examine if several soluble and cell surface signalling proteins with known functions in the cortex affect Pak1 phosphorylation on T212. We will analyse cultured cortical neurones obtained from mice lacking Cdk5 and Pak1 kinases to determine if any defects are due to the loss of phosphorylated Pak1. 2) The biological role of T212 phosphorylated Pak1 We will analyse Pak1-/- mice for the presence of cortical abnormalities. Electroporation of cortical slice cultures obtained from wild type, Cdk5-/-, p35-/- or Pak1-/- mice will be used to study the effect of wild type and mutant Pak1 proteins in proliferating or postmitotic neurones.

title: Intracellular membrane traffic in hereditary spastic paraplegia.
description: In humans, the main pathway over which voluntary motor signals are carried from the brain to the spinal cord is the corticospinal tract. Insults to the "upper motor neurons" that constitute this tract can result in a clinical picture of spastic paralysis. The hereditary spastic paraplegias (HSPs) are single gene disorders in which the axons of the corticospinal tract show progressive, length-dependant, distal degeneration after initially normal development. Functional characterisation of the responsible genes is therefore likely to reveal cellular processes that are important in long tract axonal maintenance and perhaps of relevance to common neurological diseases. More than 20 HSP loci exist and 9 of the responsible genes have been identified. Until recently, there was no discernable common underlying cellular pathological mechanism for groups of HSP conditions. However, several lines of evidence now point to defects in intracellular traffic as being the underlying cause of several different genetic types of HSP. This evidence includes the known functional role of KIF5A, a gene that I have identified as being involved in HSP, and preliminary experimental data that I have generated that implicate spastin and spartin in intracellular membrane traffic events and suggest a possible functional relationship between them. This proposal focuses on spastin and spartin and its aims are to test the hypothesis that the two proteins are functionally related components of an intracellular membrane traffic pathway that is disrupted when they are mutated. I will test this hypothesis by: a) examining whether the tissue and sub-cellular expression patterns of spastin and spartin overlap, b) further investigating preliminary experimental data that suggest physical interactions between spastin, spartin, and 2 other proteins, CHMP1.5 and gp25L2, that I identified in a yeast two- hybrid screen using spastin as bait, and which are known to be involved in intracellular membrane traffic events, c) examining in cultured mammalian cells whether knocking down expression of spastin or spartin, controlled expression of wild-type spastin or spartin, or controlled expression of mutant forms of spastin or spartin, results in any morphological or functional abnormality of intracellular membrane traffic pathways or components.

title: Mechanisms underlying the homeostatic clearance of neutrophils from the circulation via the bone marrow.
description: In man 10 neutrophils are released from the bone marrow each day. These cells have a half life in the circulation of only 6.5h. Neutrophils that are not recruited into tissues in response to an inflammatory stimulus are cleared from the circulation via the liver, spleed and bone marrow. The molecular mechanisms that regulate this clearance process are currently unknown. We have recently shown that, as neutrophils age, they dramatically upregulate their cell surface expression of CXCR4 and gain the capacity to migrate towards SDF-1a, the sole ligand for this receptor. SDF-1a is expressed constitutively in the bone marrow and we have shown that senescent neutrophils expressing CXCR4 preferentially home back to the bone marrow in a CXCR4 dependent manner, suggesting a previously undefined pathway for the clearance of senescent netrophils from the blood. In this study we will determine the relative contribution of the bone marrow, liver and spleen to the clearance of senescent neutrophils from the blood. We shall investigate whether neutrophils cleared via the bone marrow are phagocytosed and thus destroyed by bone marrow macrophages. We shall seek to identify the adhesion molecules that are involved in the trafficking of neutrophils back to the bone marrow. Finally, we shall investigate whether ageing affects the capacity of neutrophils to be recruited to sites of inflammation.

title: What mechanisms underpin variation in the skin's sensitivity to ultraviolet radiation?
description: We wish to understand the mechanisms underpinning human photoadaptation. Thereare two key unanswered questions. (1) What is the photoprotective efficacy of constitutive pigmentation compared with facultative pigmentation and (2) what are the relative roles played by pigmentary and non-pigmentary photoprotection. With respect to the second question, do those persons with low levels of pigment preferentially turn on non-pigmentary mechanisms and, ifso, why are such mechanisms apparently inadequate. We will answer these two questions by human in vivo experimentation using a range of techniques including the combination of ultraviolet transmission spectrometry of blister roofs and reflectance confocal microscopy of whole skin. Our goal is to (i) define and evaluate the biological function of the epidermis as an attenuator of ultraviolet radiation (ii) estimate the contribution the different components make (melanin, stratum corneum, and whole epidermis) (iii) see how the various elements that contribute to attenuation vary between the basal andfacultative states, and by body-site.

title: Polyadenylation and mechanisms of nuclear RNA quality control.
description: Nuclear RNA metabolism undergoes a strict quality control. An important component in all of these processing/degradation events is the nuclear exosome and a new RNA decay-activating Trf4/Air2/Mtr4 polyadenylation (TRAMP) complex. TRAMP recognizes a variety of nuclear transcripts produced by all three RNA polymerases, adds short poly(A) tails to aberrant or unstable transcripts, forming a favourable substrate for the exosome. However, it is unclear, how the aberrant RNAs are identified by the ups tream acting TRAMP. Here I propose to investigate the molecular basis for the RNA selection by the TRAMP complex. Not only known RNA substrates will be characterized in detail, but also new RNA targets identified by microarray analysis will be assessed. Potential substrates will be probed for common features that may serve as a recognition signal for targeting by the TRAMP/exosome degradation pathway. We will also investigate the molecular differences between poly(A) tails added by TRAMP and by canonical poly(A) polymerase that results in degradation or stability, respectively. The role of RNA helicase Mtr4p that is not required for the polyadenylation activity of TRAMP will be investigated. Structures of TRAMP and its subunits alone and in complex with RNA will be studied.
